excluded.reason: An orientation request issued at session start rather than a retrieval request. Nearly every memory in the corpus is a design decision, so no determinate relevant set exists.
A phrase the asker coined. Nothing in the corpus is named this, and the two labellers resolved it to different subjects.

excluded.reason: The same question asked at greater length, and ambiguous the same way.
The same orientation request, differently worded.
Ambiguous between the schema-degradation cluster and the open question of how much of a memory a response returns. The two labellers took different readings and shared no memory at all.

memories.content: Trimming records out of an exported file is not a subset export; it is the missing-record anomaly arriving through an edit that feels routine, because editing an export is a procedure the design blesses elsewhere. The difference is that re-attribution changes records in place and removes none. A removed record the target had previously agreed on is reported, named, and written for not at all.
memories.why: Loud rather than lossy, and the case is pinned by a test rather than left to the argument, because the edit feels routine at exactly the moment it is not.

memories.content: The value is called a checksum throughout, deliberately and consistently, because hash invites the cryptographic reading the sizing argument exists to rule out.
memories.why: A name is the part of a decision that survives into code written by someone who never read the reasoning, so choosing it against the misreading is cheaper than correcting the misreading later.

memories.content: The base is keyed by record and target, where the target is the export destination. One store serves every checkout of a repository, since the database is keyed on the set name alone -- but a developer may hold the same repository checked out twice on different branches, and one base per record cannot describe both. Importing from the second checkout would read the first checkout's agreement as changes arriving from origin, and every record would show up modified.
memories.why: The cost is one checksum per record per target, a few hundred kilobytes for a ten-thousand-memory set with two checkouts, so this is bookkeeping rather than scale. The rejected alternative -- one nominated target, other exports untracked -- saves state that is demonstrably cheap and makes the second checkout mis-merge silently.

memories.content: The embedder constraints are self-contained, no network at run time, filesystem-backed, permissively licensed, and Rust-native or cleanly bindable. The ladder runs from a pure-Rust static-embedding crate at 8 to 32 MB, through a pure-Rust transformer at 90 to 130 MB and substantially slower on CPU, to an ONNX-backed option whose native dependency complicates single-binary installation.
memories.why: Recording the ladder rather than only the choice is what makes the decision revisitable, since each rung names the constraint it spends.

memories.content: Memory scope is an explicit parameter on every store operation, never inferred from context. The software cannot judge whether a memory belongs to a project or stays local; that needs an understanding of what the memory means, which the LLM has.
memories.why: A personal memory committed to a public repository cannot be taken back, and the failure is asymmetric: a project memory filed as local is merely invisible, while a local memory filed as shared is published.

memories.content: The correcting convention says a changed claim is superseded by storing the corrected memory -- singular, which is wrong when only part of the memory changed. The splitting convention is a refinement of that branch rather than a separate operation, and serving them adjacently is what makes them read as one rule. Separated, a session applies the general form and bundles a half-stale correction into a single record.
memories.why: Adjacency doing semantic work is a property of a served catalog that a reference document does not have, and it is easy to lose in a reorganisation.

memories.content: Proposed: a scope resolves to exactly one store at a time and a store belongs to exactly one checkout. Stores live centrally named by a UUID assigned at creation, each records its own checkout path, and a machine-local registry records which store is live for each scope. Re-pointing a scope switches which store is live rather than redirecting one store's exports.
memories.why: What this buys is that a store has at most one export destination, so the base collapses from record-and-target back to record alone -- no target key, no path spelling to normalise, no unrecognised-target case. Two checkouts stop being one store pretending to be two replicas and become two replicas.

memories.content: The routing convention gains a third override: no shared set takes people as its subject, whatever its description claims -- a memory about a person goes with the work it concerns, or to the personal set. This closes the hole the rejected keyword clause could never have closed, because aggregation harm is a property of the set rather than of any record in it, so no rule examining one memory at a time can see it.
memories.why: It joins the compiled overrides rather than the topical descriptions because this is the one description whose faithful execution produces the artefact the principle exists to prevent, so it has to sit in text a repository cannot reach.

memories.content: Scope publishes as a string, either local or shared with a name after a colon. This is not a new encoding: the store's metadata row has used exactly that spelling since the beginning and it round-trips in both directions already. What changes is that an encoding the project already relies on internally is promoted to the tool boundary.
memories.why: It is unambiguous by construction, because the set-name rule permits letters, digits, hyphen, underscore and dot, so a set name can never contain the delimiter.

memories.content: The flag no longer collapses to a single boolean for the set. Bases are keyed by record and target, so a set can be settled against the development checkout and diverged against the review one, and is this set dirty has no answer until someone says dirty against what. That question used to block drop and no longer does.
memories.why: Its only remaining consumer is status, and there the per-target structure is not an ambiguity to resolve away but the substance of the answer, since which target is behind is exactly what a human with two checkouts wants to know.

memories.content: The set of link labels is defined in software rather than in the conventions. The deciding argument is what happens to an unrecognised label: defined in software it fails at import, where a person can see it.
memories.why: Left to the conventions it becomes a label that parses fine and that nothing knows how to traverse — a memory silently disconnected from the graph it was meant to join. Traversal is code, so the set traversal understands is the real set either way.

memories.content: Open: how conventions get extended without recompiling. Scatterhoard ships with a deliberately minimal catalog to limit the context tax, which is the right default and also creates standing pressure to add bells and whistles, and a strong convention takes runtime and revisions to get right, so the good ones will be discovered by use rather than written up front.
memories.why: That argues for two directories -- optional conventions bundled with the project and reasonably well-tested, and add-ons installed at arm's length -- and the line between them is expected to move rather than being pre-committed to a taxonomy.

memories.content: Two keywords exist only inside the alternation branches and a third only on one object branch, so removing the alternations removes all three without a separate decision. An integer type survives one client and is rewritten to a number by the other, which costs nothing and is left alone -- a note rather than a change, so the next person to see it does not read it as an oversight.
memories.why: Recording the deliberate non-change is what stops a later reader treating it as something missed.

memories.content: The runtime arrangement was re-opened and re-affirmed 2026-08-13 on better grounds. What cannot be compiled into convention text is what has to stay in the design document: the ethical half of D asks a session to weigh unknowns favourably, which is a judgement rather than a check. Convention text can name the demand and cannot verify the answer.
memories.why: The residue is the argument for the arrangement rather than a gap in it. The context objection had weakened since the catalog budget now has room spare, but the context objection was never the reason.

memories.content: A scope is bound to one checkout at a time and there is no local alias mechanism naming the same set at a second path. The capability was considered, because a reviewing session plausibly wants two checkouts at once, and it is rejected for a reason that would be very hard to recover from: a set's name is shared identity, travelling in the file header and in cross-set link targets, while an alias is per-machine state.
memories.why: A cross-set link written against an alias is meaningless on every other machine and travels in the file looking authoritative -- machine-local state laundered into shared identity, silently, by an ordinary memory write. Making it safe would require every link-writing path to resolve alias to canonical name without exception.

memories.content: Width matters more than algorithm. Comparing one record against its own stored base is a direct collision rather than a birthday problem: roughly one in four billion per changed record at 32 bits, where a miss means a memory silently stays stale, which is a correctness bug. Sixty-four bits takes it to about 5 in 10^20.
memories.why: Performance is not the deciding factor at these sizes -- a fifteen-megabyte set is tens of milliseconds of SHA-256 against one or two of a fast non-cryptographic hash, once per import or export.

memories.content: A tool that cannot do what was asked returns a result marked as an error rather than a protocol error. The model should see the failure as an answer it can act on -- a wrong set name, a missing model -- rather than as a broken call it can only retry.
memories.why: The distinction decides whether the LLM's next move is a repair or a retry, which is the difference between a session that recovers and one that loops.

memories.content: Demand A is checkability, not specificity. Specificity was the means and answerability is the end: a general characterisation like jbrown maintains XYZ is perfectly answerable by reading CODEOWNERS, while X is careless answers to nothing. The axis is evidence, not grain size.
memories.why: Getting the axis the right way round is what fixes the miscalibration that made a convention treat a plain statement of expertise as suspect. The earlier reading had specificity doing work that evidence was actually doing.

memories.content: The store's author is local state and never reaches a memory file's header. What travels is the per-memory created-by and modified-by, written from it at store time and already part of the data model.
memories.why: Keeping the distinction sharp is what stops the author being treated as set identity, which would put machine-local state into the artifact every copy has to agree on.

memories.content: Open: whether a memory needs an occurred time distinct from created. Two labels exist to express world-event order, and with no occurred field they are currently the only way to express it. A field is cheaper when absolute times are known; edges are better when only relative order is, which is the usual situation for an LLM reconstructing a history after the fact.
memories.why: The choice between a field and an edge for the same information is decided by what the writer actually knows, which is why it is deferred alongside the labels rather than settled on its own.

memories.content: Reverse derivation deliberately crosses the scope partition that keeps a query against one project's store from returning another scope's memories, because a local memory superseding a project memory means recalling the project memory should surface the local one. That is safe because the partition is protecting export, and edges live on the source memory, so exporting a project set never carries an edge that lives on a local memory.
memories.why: The partition holds where it was needed and the derivation spans where recall needs it, which is only defensible once what the partition protects is stated precisely.

memories.content: The judgment gate is governed by a hard-coded baseline set of flagging conditions, extendable and tunable via the project's local configuration, so a project can adjust when the LLM flags something without waiting on a change to the hard-coded conventions.
memories.why: Configuration rather than prompt text, deliberately: this is tuning against a bounded schema, which keeps it data rather than an instruction channel.

memories.content: How you came by a claim is a fact about the claim; how sure you feel is a fact about you, and two sessions will not agree on the second. The ladder -- watched it happen, measured or decided, inferred from evidence that fits without compelling, a reading you would check first -- is what makes two sessions land within a band of each other on the same memory.
memories.why: Measured across both live sets: 44 memories carrying five distinct values, mean 0.888, and nothing below 0.8 ever written in roughly two weeks. The previous measurement had the same five values, so seven further memories introduced none -- the field is not slowly acquiring range, and a scale whose entire observed span is its top fifth costs a judgement at every store and returns nothing.

memories.content: An operation that can destroy memories gets its own name; it is never a mode on a constructive operation. A flag makes the destructive reading one token away from the safe one -- a mode argument is chosen once, cheaply, in the middle of a longer argument list, by a caller whose attention is on the path, while a tool name has to be selected deliberately and is legible in a transcript afterward.
memories.why: This covers restore and drop and nothing else in the lifecycle. Naming is a speed bump rather than a guarantee, so it does not stand alone.

memories.content: Scatterhoard shapes what an LLM believes about a project and the people in it, and through the LLM's interaction with developers it shapes what they come to believe. A memory system sits upstream of a lot of thinking, which is why simple software can be ethically neutral and this cannot.
memories.why: It states why the principle is a technical safeguard rather than decoration. The influence is indirect and therefore easy to discount, and the second hop -- model to human -- is the one that is never counted.

memories.content: A recalled memory reports which store it came from. Once several stores answer one query, a local preference and an imported project decision arrive in the same list, and the trust difference between them is exactly what the partition exists to preserve.
memories.why: A result list that erases provenance would undo at the presentation layer the separation the storage layer was built to guarantee.

memories.content: No tombstone mechanism is needed, because forgetting can be a deleted line and git merges deletions correctly.
memories.why: The merge being considered is two branches editing one exported file, where a deletion on one side and no change on the other resolves to the deletion without ambiguity.

memories.content: A memory that was right but partial can be superseded by several memories rather than one, which is why supersession resolution reports a list of chain tips rather than a single replacement.
memories.why: The claim held as far as it went, so splitting it preserves the part that is still true instead of discarding it along with the part that is not.

memories.content: The warning does not go at session start. A session-start warning costs context, trains people to scroll past it, and frequently reaches someone who cannot act on it -- a contributor who just cloned the repository cannot fix what a maintainer committed.
memories.why: The third reason is the decisive one and the least obvious: the moment with the most attention is not the moment with the most agency, and a warning delivered to someone powerless is worse than none because it spends their trust.

memories.content: A process may fill in what a shared store does not know; it may not overwrite what the store already says. The same distinction now governs two unrelated fields -- which model built the vectors, and who the memories are attributed to -- which suggests it is a property of shared stores rather than of either feature.
memories.why: It was reached independently for the embedding model and then recognised here, and a rule arrived at twice by different routes is one worth stating at the level both instances share.

memories.content: Sharing one local store between servers makes multi-process access deliberate, so it has to be designed rather than survived. A store file is left in write-ahead mode so a writer in one server does not lock out readers in another, and a write that cannot take the lock waits rather than failing. Both are properties a shared store needs and a private one never exercises, so neither is observable from a single-process test.
memories.why: Making a previously accidental property into a requirement is what moves it from luck to design, and it is why the checks live in dedicated concurrency tests with recorded mutations beside them.

memories.content: Moving the scan into export does not cover a hand-edited memories.json committed with no re-export. That is a real path rather than a hypothetical, since renaming a forked set is specified as a hand-edit of the header.
memories.why: The answer keeps the same constraint: expose the scan as a subcommand of the Scatterhoard binary, so a pre-commit hook is one line of shell invoking something already installed rather than a program in another language.

memories.content: Export takes the path and create takes the name. A set's name is shared identity: it travels between machines in the file header and every copy agrees on it. A path is per-checkout state no other machine can see or use. Binding them at create would write machine-local state into the set's identity, and the copies would immediately disagree.
memories.why: The immediate reasons are practical -- an absolute path is wrong on the next workstation, and a repository-relative path buys uniformity at the cost of ever exporting anywhere else, including the safety copy, which by construction must go somewhere unusual. The split follows the lifetime of the information.

memories.content: Proposed 2026-08-06: the mechanical scan belongs in export rather than at the pre-commit gate. It reads the whole set, ignores the ledger and ignores authorship, so unlike the judgment gate it never needs the git diff. Everything it requires is in hand while export is serialising the records.
memories.why: It was grouped with the other two checks by proximity rather than by requirement. Moving it makes the exported response's scanned flag a fact about the export that just ran, rather than the hard-coded false it is today.

memories.content: One small corpus, written and labelled by the same author, on a single domain. The absolute recall numbers should not be trusted far -- some queries have three relevant memories, and the labels are judgement calls. The comparison is sound regardless, because both models were scored against identical labels, so systematic label bias affects them equally.
memories.why: Separating what a measurement supports from what it does not is what lets the comparison be relied on while the absolute numbers are not, and it is the discipline that keeps a spike from being over-read.

memories.content: There are two reconciliations. File against file is this checkout's exported memories against the ones arriving from origin, which git owns with a real ancestor. Store against file is the live database against whatever the file says after a pull, and nothing owned it.
memories.why: The store is a replica git has never seen, and it is the one that has been changing all session. The original phrasing assumed the store held nothing the file did not, and by the time anyone pulls it usually does.

memories.content: Visibility also scales the right way. Contradiction is rare in the present corpus but must not be assumed rare in general: supersession requires somebody to concede, and across sets two may disagree with neither side wrong and neither able to rewrite the other, leaving contradiction as the only instrument. Visibility costs one identifier per dispute and scales with that; a forced result slot each would not.
memories.why: The cross-set case is the workflow the vision is built around, so the rate in a single-set corpus is the wrong evidence to generalise from.

memories.content: If two live registrations are ever genuinely needed, the design to revisit is a typed handle that is structurally ineligible to appear as a link target -- not a second name for a scope.
memories.why: Recording the shape a future answer would have to take is what keeps the rejected option from being re-proposed in its rejected form, since the objection is to the naming rather than to the capability.

memories.content: The bases table answers given this set, which directories. Trust needs the reverse -- given this directory, which set may claim it -- and answering that means scanning every loaded store's targets. Nothing does, so nothing enforces one set per repository: two sets can both record the same directory as a target and no operation notices.
memories.why: It is also checked in only one place, since export remarks when the caller names an unrecognised directory and import does not, so import reconciles with no ancestor and says nothing.

memories.content: Requiring the reasoning behind a memory structurally favours the specific observation over the sweeping judgement, because a sweeping judgement has no reasoning to give that survives being written down.
memories.why: It is the clearest case of the principle riding on an existing field rather than a new rule, and the mechanism is mechanical rather than moral: the form makes the bad memory awkward to write.

memories.content: The budget was raised on what it is actually spending rather than on what the next convention needs. Eight thousand characters is around 1,950 tokens against context windows running from 128K on smaller local models up to about 1M, and both numbers are small at either end. A budget set at the old level would have been paid for by shrinking conventions against each other -- spending drafting effort and clarity to save something the context window does not notice.
memories.why: The token figures are the pessimistic end of the proxy, which is the right end to decide on: they assume the catalog drifts toward the vocabulary tables the constant's documentation warns about, where prose runs considerably cheaper.

memories.content: Local scaling that penalises each memory by its mean similarity to its own nearest neighbours is worse than centroid removal on its own, and combining them buys little -- under a point at five results and one hub, paid for with a 7.5-point regression at three. Not adopted for now.
memories.why: The result is also the least trustworthy in the spike, since a neighbourhood of ten against a 45-memory corpus computes the penalty over roughly a fifth of the whole set, a completely different regime from the same neighbourhood against several thousand memories. Worth re-testing at realistic scale before being ruled in or out.

memories.content: A link target cannot become a string without losing something, so it does not. The object form carries a set, an id and keywords, and those keywords exist so a reference that goes dangling has something to be re-found by -- a combined spelling would drop exactly the field that makes a dangling cross-set link recoverable. Instead the alternation moves out into sibling scalars: the target is always an id, with an optional target set and target keywords beside it.
memories.why: Objects with named properties survive both clients; only the alternation inside them does not. Nothing is lost and nothing needs a second spelling.

memories.content: The practical form of a mixed store is confusion no interface can clear up. Two memories come back ranked against each other with scores that were never comparable, and every downstream number -- the centroid, the ordering, any future floor -- is computed across a mixture. Nothing about the result looks wrong.
memories.why: A failure whose output is indistinguishable from a correct one cannot be caught by inspection, which is why the rule has to hold at write time rather than at read time.

memories.content: The review workflow does not need the reviewed set loaded, since the diff is visible to the LLM and the human alike and review questions are answered by reading rather than by recall. So there is a read-only inspect action: it reads a memory file at a caller-named path, reports its header and records, and changes nothing -- no store touched, no base recorded, no scope bound.
memories.why: Recognising that the workflow needs reading rather than loading is what keeps a whole second registration mechanism from being built for it.

memories.content: Genuine partial exchange is deferred rather than rejected, and it would need less than it looks: a recipient already handles a partial file correctly, because holding no bases for that target means records they lack arrive as new from the file and records the file omits resolve to keep-local. What is missing is a way to say which records travel, and a base rule for a target that agrees with only part of a set.
memories.why: Knowing how much of a deferred feature already works is what keeps it from being re-argued from scratch, and it locates the actual gap rather than the apparent one.

memories.content: The recall-before-storing convention closes a gap neither neighbour reached: the recall convention fires before acting, and the storing convention assumes the question is being asked for the first time. It sits second in catalog order, and the position is the argument -- the front of the catalog is the sequence of questions asked while writing one memory, and this must be settled before routing and keying, because a memory that turns out to be a correction is routed and keyed by the record it corrects.
memories.why: Catalog order carrying an argument is worth stating, because a later reorganisation on any other principle would break a dependency nothing else records.

memories.content: The code keeps unset distinguishable from set to the home, because the ordinary case must say nothing -- nobody asked for anything. A setting that looks applied while having no effect is the same shape as an author variable that is silently ignored, so it is reported. Conflating the two also made every set shadow itself in the default configuration.
memories.why: A distinction introduced for reporting turned out to fix a bug, which is a sign the distinction was real rather than cosmetic.

memories.content: Supersession is a validity relation, not a relevance relation. Every other label affects how likely a memory is to be worth surfacing; this one affects whether it is still true, which has to be resolved before ranking rather than as part of it. It is a different question that happens to be carried by an edge.
memories.why: That is why deciding it ahead of the general per-label question prejudges nothing. It also could not wait, because the whole purpose of recording a supersession is that a later session holding none of the context is told the memory is obsolete -- an edge derived correctly but never surfaced is a correction that reaches nobody.

memories.content: The property re-attribution rests on is that import writes a record exactly as the file gives it, attribution included. That is load-bearing and easy to lose: stamping an imported record with the local identity is a plausible-looking one-line change, since memorize and amend both correctly do that, and it would foreclose the route entirely while also rewriting the authorship of everyone else's memories on every pull.
memories.why: It is held by two named tests and a recorded mutation rather than by the argument, because the change that would break it looks like a consistency improvement from the side it would be made on.

memories.content: Keep the tool surface fairly simple, clear and ergonomic for the LLM. We do not know how many other MCP servers the user will load, and too many tools can be confusing. Name the tools clearly with a consistent prefix, and favour active voice and a consistent parameter order.
memories.why: Every tool added is a standing charge against the model's attention, competing with whatever other servers the user has loaded -- a cost paid in every session whether or not the tool is used.

memories.content: A tombstone removes a memory from the set going forward. It does not remove it from the history of a repository that already carries it, on every clone.
memories.why: A secret that reached a shared set must be treated as compromised whatever the current file says. The mechanical scan at the export gate is the defence, and forgetting is cleanup after that defence has already failed.

memories.content: Worth noting as an instance rather than a claim: the Golden Rule reaches runtime through the reasoning attached to memory-writing conventions, and here it did more than that -- it reversed an answer. The rest of the correction rule says a claim that changed is superseded, which would have made a retracted characterisation of a colleague permanently readable, the durability hazard produced by faithfully applying the general rule.
memories.why: The exception is in the convention text because the principle was in context while the text was being drafted, which is the mechanism working as intended.

memories.content: There are fourteen link labels, adapted from a vocabulary proven over months of daily use in a larger memory system and then tested against a corpus of real memories written before the vocabulary existed.
memories.why: Keeping the names close to that system's is deliberate, because it makes importing from it largely mechanical rather than a translation exercise.

memories.content: A derived reverse is presented as an incoming edge carrying the label as written -- recall shows that A supersedes this memory -- rather than as a synthesised inverse link on the target. Synthesising inverses would require names for directions the vocabulary deliberately does not have, and the fourteen labels were settled precisely because the LLM only ever writes outbound.
memories.why: The decisive reason is that it would destroy a distinction the vocabulary exists to carry: an authored acknowledgement of being replaced means the lower-authority side concedes, while a derived one would mean only that someone else asserted they replaced you. Conflating them loses exactly the information that made the label worth having.

memories.content: Export writes the entire set and import reconciles the entire store against the entire file. There is no partial mode, and the base machinery assumes there is none, replacing a target's whole base set rather than merging into it. Two parties exchange memories by each exporting everything and importing everything; nothing needs selecting and the sequence does not matter.
memories.why: Whole-set exchange is what makes the ordering property hold, so partiality is not a missing feature but a premise the reconciliation rests on.

memories.content: A tombstone has no free-text reason field. Attribution answers who and when, which is what an audit needs.
memories.why: A field labelled why-was-this-forgotten is where someone types the credential they were trying to remove, which reintroduces the hazard one field over from where it was just removed.

memories.content: A base carried over from a different target is not a weaker fact than no base at all -- it is a false one, and reconciliation treats the two nothing alike. With no base the two present versions are compared directly: identical converges, different is a surfaced conflict, and nothing is written over. With a wrong base that happens to equal what the store holds, the arithmetic reads store unmoved and file moved and takes the file. The store's version is replaced and nothing is reported.
memories.why: One direction costs a human a look; the other loses a memory. The asymmetry is arithmetic rather than judgement, and it is pinned as an invariant over the whole absent-base branch rather than as one more row of the table.

memories.content: Keep the convention set small until the basic system works. The catalog is deliberately minimal -- enough to exercise the mechanism, not an attempt at coverage. Expanding it is easy and tempting, and doing it before there is a working system to test conventions against would mean writing a lot of guidance nobody has watched operate.
memories.why: Two things are deferred on purpose: formalising the standing principles into conventions of their own, and a convention about how to store memories in ways that let new principles be discovered from practice.

memories.content: Since a developer using Scatterhoard is by definition working with an LLM, setup can be delegated to it: a HOWTO shipped with Scatterhoard itself, aimed at the model rather than the human. It must fit in one session, because a setup procedure that runs out of context halfway leaves a half-configured machine, which is worse than one that never started -- so bounded steps, no open-ended exploration, and a way to check the result.
memories.why: The error is the entry point: when the model is missing the message names the fix directly, so the common case never requires finding the HOWTO at all.

memories.content: Memories are data and never instructions, and that is enforceable by path rather than by inspecting content, because the loader reads one known location and treats everything else in the tree as not-memories.
memories.why: Content inspection was the wrong place to enforce it: a rule about what a file says can be defeated by what a file says, while a rule about where a file sits cannot.

memories.content: Supersession learned by derivation, from an edge on the other memory, requires that other memory's set to be loaded; without it the fact is not merely unreportable but unknown. An authored superseded-by is the memory's own data and travels with it.
memories.why: So it is the only form that survives the superseding memory being unavailable, which earns the label its place a second time and independently of the trust argument.

memories.content: Import reconciles a file against a store that may have diverged from it, keeping a memory the store holds that the file has never carried. Restore replaces: the file becomes the store and local divergence is discarded on purpose, serving the case where the store is corrupt or being rebuilt and reconciling against it would mean merging against content nobody trusts.
memories.why: The same decision-placement test that collapsed export and backup gives the opposite answer here, which is worth being explicit about because the surface pressure runs the other way.

memories.content: Two better moments carry the warning: the export review gate as the primary home, where the local user is about to add to the repository and is in a position to act, and once on first encountering a given project, so a genuinely suspicious file is not sitting unmentioned until the first export.
memories.why: The export-review ledger is already local-only per-machine state tracking whether something has been dealt with, so it can carry the first-encounter flag without new machinery.

memories.content: A destructive operation takes a path and writes the set there before destroying it. Not a refusal, a save. Drop and restore share one rule, and the guarantee sharpens from cannot discard unexported memories to cannot discard memories without first writing them somewhere the caller named.
memories.why: Refusal is worst exactly when the operation matters most, since restore is reached for when something is broken and a human is under pressure. The safety copy is also more useful than a clean flag: the exported format diffs well, so a pre-restore copy can be compared against the restored set and individual memories cherry-picked back.

memories.content: The scope type has no Default implementation, ever. Deriving one would silently reintroduce exactly the inference that explicit scope rules out.
memories.why: Once a decision's proper home is settled, the type system should make the wrong placement unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged, so the rule lives in the compiler rather than in anyone's memory.

memories.content: The fix has to be a design in which the order does not matter, rather than documentation telling users which order to use.
memories.why: A rule whose violation is undetectable and unrecoverable cannot be discharged by instruction. Stating the requirement this way is what rules out the whole family of answers that add a warning.

memories.content: Open: whether a set should be able to declare its own keyword conventions, via a reserved keyword that is the obvious sibling of the topics memory routing already matches against.
memories.why: Raised as the natural extension of a mechanism that had just been built, which is the moment such a question is cheapest to notice and most likely to be over-generalised.

memories.content: Because identifiers are time-ordered, ordering by id and ordering by creation time are the same order, so there is one sort key rather than two that can disagree.
memories.why: The file format asks for a consistent export order to keep merge diffs small and names either key, and a single key removes the possibility of the two drifting apart.

memories.content: With the base, the incoming record's checksum and the store record's checksum, reconciliation is a five-way decision per id: both unchanged is nothing to do; file changed alone takes the file's version; store changed alone keeps local, which exports later; both changed but file equals store is independent convergence, accepted and cleared; both changed and different is a genuine conflict, surfaced.
memories.why: The convergence row matters more than it looks: without it, two people making the same correction produces a conflict, and conflict stops meaning anything.

memories.content: No key removes the need for the warning. Canonicalising a path collapses spellings but does not survive the checkout being renamed or moved, which orphans every base just as thoroughly and reads as a target never seen before. Since no key eliminates the unrecognised-target case, the load-bearing fix is that an unrecognised target is always said out loud, and normalisation is hygiene that reduces how often it fires.
memories.why: Separating the load-bearing fix from the hygiene is what stops normalisation being mistaken for the solution and the warning being dropped once paths are tidy.

memories.content: Gap-filling and mismatch re-embedding diverge in precisely the case the safety argument anticipated. Concurrent sweeps converging on identical rows -- duplicated work rather than a race -- holds for gaps, where both servers compute the same missing vectors, and fails for mismatches, where each server's rebuild invalidates the other's.
memories.why: Convergence versus oscillation is the difference, and it is not visible from either process. So gap-filling stays automatic because it converges, and mismatch re-embedding becomes explicit because it oscillates and the information needed to choose lives with the human who configured both servers.

memories.content: The first real two-server run showed the model-mismatch case producing an unbounded loop: two servers with different models each re-embedded the whole store on the other's turn, indefinitely, and a single recall was enough to trigger it.
memories.why: The earlier reasoning was sound and rested on a premise that run falsified. Neither the LLM nor the human holds information that would justify leaving a store half-embedded is true of a single decider; with two servers, the other server's configuration is exactly that information, and neither server holds it.

memories.content: A missing embedding model does not fail the call. Recall returns what it can and says, in words the model will read, that the store could not be searched by meaning and that memory should be treated as unconsulted rather than empty.
memories.why: Treating an unsearchable store as empty is the reassuring failure the loud-degradation rule exists to prevent, and the tool layer is where that rule has to be honoured.

memories.content: The re-embed always proceeds, carrying the warning with it. The harms are asymmetric: what the check protects is derived state rebuilt in under a second, while a wrong refusal costs semantic recall itself. Blocking a capability to protect cheap rebuildable state is the wrong way round.
memories.why: The lockout is concrete rather than hypothetical. Decommission the second server and try to restore recall with the model that remains: the history says that model was already displaced, so a re-entry check refuses it, while the recorded model is one nothing on the machine can supply. A store must not be reachable into a state its own tool surface cannot repair.

memories.content: Every vector in a store is produced by that store's recorded model, or the memory has none. A store never holds vectors from two models at once, and changing the model resets the vector of every memory embedded with a different one.
memories.why: The rule that forces this is already stated for stores searched together, since one query is embedded once and scored against all of them. That reasoning does not weaken inside a single store -- it is the same defect at a smaller radius, and worse there, because the union check has at least somewhere to notice while within one store there is no seam to inspect.

memories.content: If a candidate's final score were only its own similarity to the query, traversal would return nothing that a larger limit would not return sooner and more cheaply -- and it would penalise the very case it exists for. A memory is often relevant because of its relation rather than its wording: the measurement supporting a decision, the constraint that decision rests on. Those are precisely the memories whose content does not match the query.
memories.why: This is measured rather than supposed: a memory carrying a rare identifier ranked below an unrelated memory on content similarity. So a reached memory carries a decayed share of its seed's score and the query-similarity term shapes the result on top of it.

memories.content: A refusal comes with a way out in three parts, all needed since any two leave the LLM stuck: status reports the model state honestly, naming recorded and loaded identity; the recall refusal names the remedy; and the sets tool gains a re-embed action that rebuilds every vector with the model in hand, states which model that is, and reports how many were rebuilt.
memories.why: Cost is not the objection, since a full rebuild of a ten-thousand-memory set is sub-second. What the explicit step buys is that a rebuild happens because someone chose it, and two servers then refuse rather than fight -- a visible standoff instead of an invisible loop.

memories.content: Each convention carries two kinds of supporting text and they are not the same. Reinforcement is served alongside the convention every time it is used, reinforcing it in the moment and clarifying when it applies, and it lives in the data. Update-time context is the background someone needs when changing the convention, and it lives in source comments, which are never served.
memories.why: The test that sorts them: does this text reinforce the convention at the moment of use? If yes it is reinforcement; if it only helps someone deciding whether to revise the convention, it is a comment.

memories.content: Routing failure and export failure turn out to be the same failure. A local set is never published, so a project memory misfiled as personal is not merely untidy: the export convention can never see it, and it stays on one machine permanently. That is what the eighteen misplaced memories were.
memories.why: Two conventions that looked independent share a failure mode, which is the kind of coupling that only appears when the catalog is read end to end rather than entry by entry.

memories.content: The forker's own machine needs drop then import, because the local database records the old name in its metadata and editing the file does not reach it. That is the drop-plus-import path working as intended, and the save-first rule means the old set is written out before it goes.
memories.why: A consequence not obvious from the edit itself, and the kind that turns a one-line change into a procedure.

memories.content: It does not follow that add-on cost is invisible. A user choosing well needs to know what a convention costs before enabling it, which is a reporting problem rather than an enforcement one, and is open.
memories.why: Distinguishing the enforcement question from the reporting question is what let the first be settled while the second stays open, instead of both waiting on each other.

memories.content: A local set is still written to a file, for backup and restore. That is a different operation from export and does not go through export eligibility, which continues to answer none for local scope.
memories.why: Serialising a set and being allowed to publish it are separate questions, and only the second is what export eligibility decides. A memory set that cannot be backed up is one bad disk away from being gone.

memories.content: Unresolved design questions are gathered from across the subject files so they do not get lost, and a question resolved elsewhere is moved out into its subject file with the reasoning recorded there. A resolved question often leaves work behind, and that work goes to the backlog -- decided, not yet built.
memories.why: The boundary in the other direction: if the work cannot start until someone chooses between two designs, it stays a question here however concrete it sounds. Resolving a question and finding nothing implements the answer is the normal case rather than a discovery worth burying.

memories.content: Keyword search is search -- it produces ranked results and resolves validity exactly as semantic recall does -- so it belongs on the same tool as a second way of asking the same question. Direct reference is retrieval, and it behaves differently in the one way that matters: it is exempt from supersession substitution.
memories.why: Making it a parameter would give one tool two contradictory behaviours depending on which argument was supplied, with a superseded memory swapped for its replacement or returned as asked, decided by a field. That is a worse cost than one extra tool.

memories.content: The shared scope variant was called Project until 2026-08-04. It was renamed because a shared set needs a name and an export destination but not a repository.
memories.why: A cross-project set of coding lessons made the old name read as a claim the type never made, and a name that overstates what a type guarantees misleads exactly the reader who trusts it.

memories.content: The cost is one extra call when a caller genuinely wants both, and the loss of one real signal: a memory found by both paths is stronger evidence of relevance than one found by either, and splitting hides it. That is recorded as the reason to revisit under hybrid search.
memories.why: Naming the signal that the refusal discards is what keeps the open question honest rather than letting the decision look free.

memories.content: A convention belongs in the built-in catalog if a user who does not know it exists would be worse off. Held as a test to try against candidates rather than a settled rule, since the division is expected to move as the catalog grows and a criterion adopted before it has judged anything real is one nobody has watched operate.
memories.why: What recommends it is that it discriminates without needing a taxonomy of subject matter, and the asymmetry it encodes is the reason it works: the cost of a missing built-in is invisible to the person paying it, and the cost of an unnecessary one is not. So the test puts the burden of proof where the failure is silent.

memories.content: A choice with no consequence produces inconsistent data, because different sessions decide it differently and nothing ever corrects them.
memories.why: It also spends context making an arbitrary choice look principled, which costs twice: once in the tokens and once in the false impression that the value means something.

memories.content: Demand D has two halves that are different kinds of claim. The first is ordinary epistemics -- a generalisation reaches past its evidence by construction, so the unknowns are the whole question. The second is the genuinely ethical half and is scoped tightly: it governs the inference from evidence to motive and nothing else.
memories.why: Separating them is what makes the ethical clause small enough to defend. It also answers the well-evidenced unfavourable record, where four failing PRs are a fact D leaves alone and does not test their work is a generalisation past those four points.

memories.content: A store's identity and its location must be separable, because the location changes and the identity must not. Identity is a UUID fixed at creation and never rewritten, before any checkout is involved, which is what lets an unattached set exist at all. Location is a path recorded in the store's metadata -- a label to be corrected rather than a key to be matched, so a moved checkout is one row to update rather than an orphaned store.
memories.why: The alternative was encoding the path in the filename, which is legible with no tooling but must be renamed when a checkout moves or it states something false. A filename that confidently asserts the wrong path is worse than an opaque one, because nothing prompts a reader to doubt it.

memories.content: Vectors are computed locally and never appear in the exported memory file. The export carries content, why, keywords, links and metadata, and an importing machine computes its own vectors from that content.
memories.why: Several hundred floats per memory would defeat the consistent export ordering chosen to keep merge diffs small, and the field-level merge driver would be reconciling vector noise with no meaningful merge semantics -- two branches re-embedding the same memory produce trivially different floats with no correct resolution.

memories.content: This is not a cheaper substitute for the registry; it is the registry with its single fact derived rather than stored, which is the move already made for every other fact considered. A recorded registry earns its keep only when two stores can claim one scope in the same place and something must choose between them, which is the runtime switchboard. Removing the switchboard removes the reason to write the fact down.
memories.why: Framing it as derivation rather than replacement is what keeps the registry's reasoning available if the switchboard ever comes back.

memories.content: With one JSON object per line, two branches editing different fields of the same memory -- one adding a link, the other bumping confidence -- still look to git like two edits to the same line, so plain line-based merging over-reports conflicts even though the changes are logically compatible.
memories.why: The weakness is a direct consequence of the one-record-per-line choice, so it is the price of a format that diffs well rather than an oversight, and it bounds what the merge driver below has to fix.

memories.content: A caller may still say back up my local memories in words; the tool they reach for is export with local scope, and the response should say the gate was skipped and why, so the difference stays visible where it matters -- in the result, not in the surface.
memories.why: Collapsing two tool names into one loses nothing only if the distinction reappears in the output. Putting it there rather than in the surface is what keeps the collapse honest.

memories.content: Reading a set of memories when memories for that project already exist raises two classes of question: memories that used to exist but were deliberately forgotten or superseded, and entirely new memories created locally, such as during work on the current branch.
memories.why: Naming the two classes separately is what keeps the answer from being a single overwrite rule, since one class is about absence meaning something and the other is about presence that the file has never seen.

memories.content: Decided 2026-08-11: never keep a reconciliation base you cannot prove. A migration keeps nothing where the store has no targets, keeps the single target where the choice is forced and the spellings provably denote one directory, and where there are two or more keeps at most the destination and drops every other target's rows outright.
memories.why: The open question had weighed adopting the most-recent target against refusing and asking as comparable options. They are not, and measuring the difference mostly answers the question.

memories.content: The hazard the principle guards is memories that characterise collaborators. A set accumulates them, and the system makes them worse than ordinary human friction does.
memories.why: Locating the hazard precisely is what turns a sentiment into a design concern: the harm is created by the system's own mechanics rather than being a general worry about unkindness.

memories.content: An edge cannot suppress a memory it does not outrank. A local memory may supersede a project memory, but a project memory may not suppress a local one, because that inverts the trust gradient.
memories.why: Project memories arrive over an untrusted channel and local ones do not. Exploiting this today would need a local memory's id and those are not public, which is exactly why it is worth making structural: relying on identifiers being unguessable is the kind of incidental protection this design has refused before.

memories.content: Whether a record changed locally is already answered by comparing it against its base, so the per-record dirty flag is an optimisation that keeps status from rehashing the set. The base is the truth and the flag is derived from it, rebuildable by rehashing.
memories.why: Stated in that order deliberately: two independent facts that can disagree is the failure this project keeps filing, and a cache with a known source is not that.

memories.content: Most anticipated needs are configuration rather than prose. The one concrete use case in the design so far, adjusting the export gate's flagging conditions, is tuning rather than instruction, and a bounded config schema covers it. Nothing currently needs a prompt channel, so none is provided.
memories.why: It answers the obvious objection that refusing a prompt channel will block real needs, by checking the needs actually on the table rather than imagined ones.

memories.content: The exported file is ordered by memory id, which for time-ordered identifiers is also creation order, so the same content always produces the same bytes and a newly stored memory appends near the end rather than landing in the middle.
memories.why: Diff size is what determines whether a human can review a memory merge, and unstable ordering makes every export look like a rewrite.

memories.content: Encode the signal as identity, not as elapsed time. A timestamp asks the reader to infer contention from a duration -- a weak signal an LLM reasons about poorly, since the same four minutes is alarming in a tug-of-war and unremarkable otherwise. Instead the store keeps a bounded history of the model identities it has held, and the re-embed tests whether the requested model is one that was already displaced.
memories.why: That is a cycle, and cycle detection is exact -- the same shape as the supersession cycle handling, which is precedent rather than a new idea. The first re-embed is unremarkable; only re-entry is evidence, and it escalates with the count.

memories.content: The superseded-by label exists because of the trust rule: it is how the lower-authority side records its own obsolescence without anyone reaching across the boundary.
memories.why: Writing a supersession onto the higher-authority memory is impossible when that set is not this machine's to edit, and is the trust inversion the rule forbids even when it is possible.

memories.content: The export convention was split in two after its old phrasing turned out to carry three things: exporting the file, reviewing the resulting diff, and an unstated assumption that the memories worth exporting had been captured at all. The third is the one that hid -- a convention that reads as though it produces memories can only ship ones that already exist, and reports success on an unchanged file when nothing was captured.
memories.why: Placement follows the information: at commit time the knowledge has faded and you are reconstructing, while at the end of the work it is fresh -- and the diff and the commit only exist at commit time.

memories.content: Self-containment serves three goals at once: it keeps the server easy to adopt, and it allays fears about personal information being exported, because a system with no external components has nowhere to send anything.
memories.why: The privacy argument is the one that is easy to miss, and it is structural rather than a promise. A design that cannot phone home does not need to be trusted not to.

memories.content: The override is scoped to shared sets on purpose. The personal set is the acknowledged catch-all and can accumulate cross-topic memories about one person, but it never travels, so the durability and reach mechanics are weaker on one person's own machine -- and widening the override to every set would forbid the fallback the convention's own next sentence depends on.
memories.why: One consequence is accepted rather than overlooked: this forbids a team set whose charter is personnel notes, weighed against the argument that a charter is visible by design and a tool refusing to hold them is making a policy choice its users did not ask for.

memories.content: Partly resolved: recall and lookup now return the memory's complete field set through a single view type shared by every tool, so a returned memory carries its own supersession edge and the walk the design describes is available to a caller -- the code caught up to the design rather than the other way round. What remains is the budget question of how much to return.
memories.why: The reason the full field set went in first was corpus integrity rather than caller convenience, which is worth recording because it explains an ordering that otherwise looks like it optimised the wrong thing.

memories.content: A counter was the candidate for gating restore by comparing a file's version against the store's. It is the wrong instrument for the case that matters: a version comparison reads the store to decide whether the store may be replaced, which is unavailable precisely when the store is corrupt.
memories.why: That sentence generalised further than it was written to -- applied to the dirty flag itself it removes the flag from the destructive path entirely. The counter argument was right about a class and was only ever applied to one member of it.

memories.content: With re-pointing settled at startup rather than at runtime, the registry's one fact becomes derivable from where a store's file sits, and the runtime switchboard two processes could fight over is gone -- and with it the question this document called its largest gap. Two of the registry's three motivations survive, and neither is served by placement: the per-target base, and binding a set name to a checkout.
memories.why: Recording which motivations survive a supersession is what stops the whole proposal being discarded with the part that was replaced.

memories.content: No keyword count is specified. Practice already runs three to six with no rule saying so, so a number would describe sessions rather than change them -- and a choice whose answer changes nothing should not exist. How many keywords a memory needs is information that lives with the memory being written.
memories.why: The decision-placement test applied to a convention rather than to a parameter, which is the same test doing the same work one layer up.

memories.content: The routing convention asks what the memory is about, not what you were doing. That distinction is what the data demanded: you are working on the project either way, so what am I doing routes everything to the project set, and the general lessons that happen to be learned there get filed with it.
memories.why: The gap was real and measured -- of 26 memories in the personal set, roughly eighteen were project knowledge, six general engineering lessons, one a genuine working preference and one a leftover test fixture, with four having twins already in the project set.

memories.content: The export response carries a note beside the scanned flag, because false was true for two unrelated reasons and said which was which for neither: a local export skips the gate by design, having nothing to publish, while a shared export skips it only because no scan exists.
memories.why: The distinction gets sharper rather than redundant once the scan lands -- a shared export that genuinely went unscanned must not read like a local one that never needed scanning -- so the note is not scaffolding to remove.

memories.content: A person forgets an irritation; a memory system does not. A moment of frustration, once recorded, becomes a permanent characterisation that outlives the situation that produced it.
memories.why: This is the first of the three mechanics that make recorded characterisations worse than remembered ones, and it is the one with no human analogue at all -- forgetting is the mechanism that ordinarily limits the damage.

memories.content: Identity travels, location does not is not violated by the registry. That rule objects to binding a path into a set's identity, where copies on other machines would disagree. The registry is explicitly machine-local and never enters a header. Recording a path locally was always fine; publishing it was not.
memories.why: Checking a new mechanism against a rule it superficially contradicts, and finding the rule narrower than it looked, is what keeps a principle from being either violated or over-applied.

memories.content: The budget constant does double duty: it is also the default page size for a conventions request. That coincidence is what makes the catalog reliably serve in a single page -- the ceiling on its size and the default page size are the same number, so a catalog that passes the budget test cannot need a second page. Changing one changes the other.
memories.why: A coupling that is load-bearing and invisible from either side is worth knowing before touching the constant, since the failure would be a catalog that silently needs paging.

memories.content: The unconditional safety copy survives but its argument has to be rewritten. One leg does not survive here, since one destination means one base and a well-defined answer to whether a set is dirty. The decision stands on the leg that does -- a base records a past agreement rather than the current contents of a file -- and on two cases this design creates: an unattached set has no destination and so no base at all, making every record unsaved by construction, and an orphaned store can report clean because it genuinely agreed with its file before the checkout was deleted.
memories.why: The orphan is where a flag is actively wrong: a flag-gated drop would skip the safety copy in the one case where the memories exist nowhere else.

memories.content: A recall-gloss convention is wanted and not yet drafted: when the LLM surfaces a recalled memory to the human it should lead with a short gloss built from the memory's context field rather than restating content cold, which is the behaviour that actually solves the friction the context field exists to address. It also needs guidance on what is worth capturing into context in the first place, kept loose rather than a fixed schema.
memories.why: A convention whose text is written but not yet served is a normal state and is a backlog entry rather than an omission, and the same holds for one identified but undrafted.

memories.content: The old person clause -- record the specific observation rather than a characterisation -- carried the verdict and lost the axis, so it read a plain statement of expertise as suspect when the hazard is an unfavourable claim on thin evidence. The new clause states the demands directly: record what a later session's work needs, record what you observed rather than what you concluded, name where it can be checked, and before generalising account for what you do not know.
memories.why: Three open questions were settled together because they were one question, and the clauses carrying the principle had each been compiled from its conclusions with the derivation never written down.

memories.content: At the file layer git's ancestor-aware three-way merge handles both hard cases for free: a deliberately forgotten memory is delete-versus-unmodified, treated as a clean delete, while delete-versus-modified is a genuine conflict; and divergent edits to the same memory are flagged correctly without Scatterhoard reconstructing merge semantics itself.
memories.why: It is worth stating what git gets right, because the sections that follow are about the half it cannot see, and the boundary between them is the whole design.

memories.content: Someone who genuinely needs to keep sensitive data near a memory puts it in a file and stores a memory that refers to the file. The memory carries the pointer; the file carries the secret and never enters the set.
memories.why: Without a sanctioned alternative the rule gets broken by whoever has a real need, because the need does not go away when the prohibition arrives. Indirection satisfies the need and keeps the exported artifact clean, since a path is not a credential.

memories.content: The tools are conventions, memorize, recall, lookup, correct and sets: the vision's store and recall, the convention loading required before anything else happens, and the tools that manage what has already been stored. Nothing else until it earns a place. They are listed in the order a session uses them rather than alphabetically.
memories.why: A heading over this table read three tools while the table listed four, and kept reading that way as the surface grew to six. A count in a heading is a hand-maintained copy of the length of the table beneath it, in the smallest possible form.

memories.content: Content and why together are the memory's claim: what it asserts and the reasoning that makes it judgeable. Keywords, links, context and confidence are apparatus.
memories.why: That single line does most of the work of deciding which correction operation applies, because it separates what someone believed from how the record was filed.

memories.content: The second measured failure is vocabulary drift: a store holding two spellings of one idea as separate singletons, and a term beside two variants of itself. A keyword only gathers when it matches the spelling already in use, so a second name for one idea splits a subject into two searches that each return half of it. Hence recall the keyword before coining it -- a mechanism that costs one call and works with no embedding model loaded.
memories.why: One such split was produced during the same session, an hour before the convention was drafted and with nothing in the catalog to prevent it, which is as fair a test of the need as the evidence gets.

memories.content: The scope-topics keyword is the first operational keyword -- one Scatterhoard reads rather than one a human searches by -- so the prefix is reserved: keywords beginning with the project's short prefix belong to Scatterhoard, and a project using one for its own content is making an error rather than creating an ambiguity.
memories.why: That is the same namespace claim the project already makes three times over, for environment variables, tool names and the reserved directory, and the existing prefix was chosen over a new abbreviation for exactly that continuity.

memories.content: An exported file is a memory set, so every memory in it has the same scope, and recording scope per memory would create a value that can disagree with the file containing it plus a check to keep the two in step.
memories.why: A memory read out of a file is therefore scope-less as a value: it acquires its scope from the store it is loaded into, and storage is partitioned by scope already, so nothing downstream has to consult a field to know which set it is working with.

memories.content: What carries the weight is that the message is directive rather than descriptive. A third alternation between two models is a fact the reader may or may not act on; saying that two servers are configured with different models, that this will keep recurring until that is fixed, and to raise it with the human rather than re-running says what to do -- and is available in a warning exactly as much as in a refusal.
memories.why: This removes the override entirely, along with the question nobody could answer about it: an LLM meeting a refusal that names an override is fairly likely to simply use it. With nothing to refuse there is nothing to override.

memories.content: Uniform expansion is licensed by the re-scoring, not by itself. A walk that wanders out of the sense a query intended is harmless because the cut re-scores everything -- think of ice alongside computers, where a related edge into frozen water is picked up by the expansion and dropped by the ranker. Were ranking ever to run on graph distance alone, that same crude expansion would become a defect.
memories.why: The tolerance for a rough walk is bought by the ranker and is not a property of the walk, which is a dependency rather than a happy accident and constrains any later change.

memories.content: Open: whether recall should ever combine semantic and keyword search into one ranking. The combination was removed because it integrated nothing -- two independent searches stapled together, duplicating payload, putting two scales in one response, with no honest ordering -- and separating them makes those unrepresentable. But separation is the conservative answer rather than the best one, and a memory found by both paths is stronger evidence of relevance than one found by either, a signal that now exists nowhere.
memories.why: Recording what a conservative answer discards is what keeps it revisitable, since the argument that removed the combination says nothing against a genuinely integrated ranking.

memories.content: Published tuning for graph-augmented retrieval is not a shortcut past this. Nearly all of it concerns graphs derived from text automatically, where the edges are statistical; here every edge was authored deliberately by the writer of one of its endpoints. Constants would not transfer, and borrowing them would reintroduce exactly the unmeasured numbers this design has avoided elsewhere.
memories.why: The temptation is strongest precisely when a corpus is not yet available, which is when borrowed constants would be least checkable.

memories.content: Which sets are loaded, and which have unexported changes, are the two halves of one question, which is what makes status and dirty-tracking one feature rather than two. It also closes a defect with no other fix: a caller told to check the set name has nothing to check against.
memories.why: Recognising two requirements as one question is what keeps the tool surface small, and the surface staying small is a standing constraint rather than an aesthetic.

memories.content: Most of the difficulty in the per-label question came from asking one mechanism to do two jobs. The walk generates candidates and the embedding judges them: expansion from the seeds is uniform and symmetric, every label crossed the same way in both directions, decaying with distance and with nothing else. It makes no attempt to judge relevance, because the graph does not know relevance -- it knows what some author thought worth connecting.
memories.why: Relevance is judged afterwards by scoring each candidate against the query, which needs no information the store does not already hold, since every memory has a vector and so does the query.

memories.content: Create is a distinct operation, not a special case or mode of import.
memories.why: Import reconciles a file against a store; create brings a set into existence with nothing to reconcile against. Folding them together would mean import inventing a store on a typo, which silently splits a set -- and refusing an unknown set name was right for exactly that reason.

memories.content: The design used to live in a single file and is now split by subject so each topic can be found, linked and edited independently, with the old file pointing at the index.
memories.why: A single design document makes every cross-reference a section anchor inside one file, which is what made the reference structure invisible; splitting it is what let the links between subjects become the thing this corpus is built from.

memories.content: The human partner settled the assumption this rests on: a restart is acceptable for changing which sets a server reaches. Power users who need a layout at all will tweak it rarely, and on one client a server can be reconnected without starting a new session, while on another it is an application restart.
memories.why: The whole startup-rather-than-runtime resolution depends on this being acceptable, so it is worth recording as a decision made rather than a convenience assumed.

memories.content: It must be possible to use Scatterhoard with no network connection.
memories.why: This rules out a hosted embedding API no matter how much better its vectors would be, and it is the constraint that makes the embedder choice a local-model question rather than a quality comparison.

memories.content: Decided 2026-08-06: the save is unconditional and no flag gates it. The fact the guard needs is whether any memory's current content exists in no file, and the base cannot answer it -- the base records an agreement between two particular replicas, which is a claim about a past moment rather than about what is on disk now.
memories.why: Two collapses were considered and both over-read it in opposite directions. Dirty against any target reads not yet agreed with every replica as not saved, so a two-checkout set is dirty whenever either is behind and the gate stops discriminating. Dirty against every target is closer but claims what it cannot support, since a branch switch changes the file on disk with the base untouched. Neither is a tuning problem, so the gate is removed rather than tuned.

memories.content: Another project gets a cross-project set's memories because the developer imports the set, not the project. A set loaded on a machine participates in recall for every session on that machine, so nothing is copied into the other project's repository -- the lessons live in one place and are read by many projects rather than being vendored into each and drifting.
memories.why: Copying memories between sets is a different operation, deliberately not designed here. It would need an answer for what happens when the source set later changes, which is the problem vendoring always has.

memories.content: This recovers for free the distinction collapsed when backup was merged into export. The two operations were rightly made one, because the caller states a scope and everything else follows from it; now backup-versus-export follows from whether the path is the set's home, which is a fact the software already holds. Neither a second tool nor a mode argument.
memories.why: A distinction that returns as a derived fact rather than as a parameter is the shape the decision-placement test keeps producing, and it is worth noticing when a later mechanism restores something an earlier one gave up.

memories.content: Forgetting writes a tombstone: a line carrying the memory's id and the attribution of the act, and nothing else.
memories.why: The earlier reasoning that a deleted line would do was sound for the merge it considered and does not cover reconciling a store against a file, where a memory absent from the file might never have been in it.

memories.content: The conventions may establish specific ways of tagging certain information -- gathering evidence on a bug across multiple merges, or tagging work associated with a branch. It should be possible to generate seed memories purely through keyword search, and maybe to disable graph traversal during the search in order to surface only memories tagged that specific way.
memories.why: Keyword search answers a different question from similarity: an exact tag is a claim about membership rather than about meaning, and traversal from such a seed would dilute exactly the precision that made the tag worth writing.

memories.content: A store owns the local facts about itself, and the environment supplies a default rather than the truth. A variable read at process start is the wrong home for anything that must stay consistent across processes.
memories.why: It is what git already does -- identity is per repository, for exactly this reason, because one person legitimately contributes under different identities -- and it is the same pattern already applied to the checkout path.

memories.content: Becoming more or less sure of an identical claim is a recalibration of apparatus, not a new belief, so a confidence change alone is an amendment.
memories.why: Superseding for it would put two near-identical memories in a chain differing by one float, which is precisely the duplicate-the-content-to-fix-metadata failure that makes chains less useful. If the reason for the change is itself worth keeping, that is a new memory about the evidence.

memories.content: A general lesson with a project-specific instance has no single right destination, and the convention says to store both rather than choose. This project's own store makes the case concrete: its largest single source of defects is a general principle whose evidence is entirely local to the project, and two memories had already been split that way by instinct.
memories.why: A rule that codifies what careful practice was already doing is the cheapest kind to adopt, because the behaviour is known to be workable before it is required.

memories.content: The first of two independent checks is a deterministic scan for the prohibited data categories. It runs on the full exported set every export cycle, and is not scoped by authorship or by the ledger.
