memories.why: Whether a secret leaked in because of something the local user wrote or something merged in from elsewhere does not change the risk of committing it, and the check is cheap enough to run unconditionally.

memories.content: A missing model degrades loudly, never silently. Semantic search is one of three recall paths, and keyword search, direct-id lookup and traversal all still work without a model, so Scatterhoard can run without one -- but recall must say that semantic search is unavailable.
memories.why: A quiet degradation is precisely the failure the recall convention warns about: memory that is not really being consulted, while the session believes it is.

memories.content: Inspection is the one operation that should read a header without trusting it. Everywhere else a file's claimed scope can only agree with what the path already established, which is the rule that closes the privilege-escalation channel. Inspection grants no trust at all, since nothing is loaded and so nothing can be escalated into, so it should accept a file claiming any scope and report what it claims, labelled as a claim.
memories.why: That is strictly more useful for review, since seeing a fork's header still asserting the upstream set name is exactly the thing a reviewer needs to notice.

memories.content: An author update applies to future writes only. Memories already stored keep the attribution they were written with, and the response says how many carry a different author, so the split is visible rather than discovered later.
memories.why: Reporting the residue at the moment of the change is what keeps a partial fix from being mistaken for a complete one.

memories.content: A pruned tombstone is indistinguishable from the missing-record anomaly, which is a good argument for not pruning until there is a concrete reason -- and given that forgetting is expected to be rare next to superseding, there may never be one.
memories.why: It records a constraint that a future space-saving change would otherwise discover by breaking the anomaly detector, which is the kind of coupling that is invisible from the code being changed.

memories.content: The sibling shape does make an invalid combination constructible -- a target set with no target. That is the objection an earlier issue raised, and it is accepted here for a reason that did not apply then: the alternative is not a more precise schema but an emptier one, since the client that would have enforced the distinction is the client that discards it.
memories.why: A combination the schema no longer forbids is refused by the parser and named in the response, which moves the guarantee rather than dropping it.

memories.content: Naming an already-held memory removes it from the results but not from seed selection or graph traversal. A memory the LLM already holds and is now querying around is the best available seed -- a known-relevant, already-validated anchor into the right neighbourhood -- and its links remain valid connective tissue, so excluding it from the walk would disconnect whatever lies beyond it.
memories.why: So this is a recall improvement rather than merely a cost saving: the caller contributes free high-quality seeds by declaring what it already has.

memories.content: Each record carries the checksum it had when the store and the file last agreed, called the base. It is local per-replica state, living in the store beside the vectors and the export-review ledger, never in the file, because it records an agreement between two particular replicas and means nothing to a third.
memories.why: Keeping it out of the file is what makes it correct rather than merely private: a base written into the exchanged artifact would be read by a third replica as a fact about their agreement, which it is not.

memories.content: The combined call ran the two paths independently and stapled the results together. It integrated nothing, so it produced nothing a caller could not get from two calls, while creating three problems at once: a memory found both ways came back twice in full, measured at roughly 1,100 duplicated bytes carrying about 30 bytes of new information; the response held two scales with no stated relationship; and any attempt to order the combined result had to either invent a blended ranking or exile keyword-only hits to the bottom.
memories.why: Refusing the combination makes all three unrepresentable rather than fixed, which is the correctness-by-construction posture the rest of the design takes.

memories.content: Reconciliation compares records by checksum, and what the checksum covers is not the line as written but a canonical serialisation: the fields this build knows, keys in sorted order, no insignificant whitespace.
memories.why: Hashing the raw line would let any cosmetic difference — a merge tool normalising whitespace, a writer emitting keys in a new order — read as a content change on every record in the file, turning the next reconciliation into one enormous false conflict.

memories.content: If the user is working on multiple projects the LLM does not reload the conventions, which would waste context, but it does load the second project's memories and keep both in storage, using memory steering to put the correct memories in the correct sets.
memories.why: Conventions are the same everywhere while memory sets are not, so the two halves of session start have different multiplicities. Treating them as one step would either waste context or lose a set.

memories.content: A publication read by software you do not control has to degrade into something usable, not into something empty. The precise statement can be the best answer available; it cannot be the only one.
memories.why: The general form is worth keeping because it is not about JSON Schema at all -- it applies wherever a producer states something precisely to a consumer whose handling it cannot observe.

memories.content: Measured over both live sets: 109 distinct keywords over 34 memories, 4.7 per memory, and 71% of the distinct keywords used exactly once. The singletons divide sharply rather than uniformly -- one group names one identifiable thing precisely, which is the case exact match exists for, while the other is broad words coined once, gathering nothing and too vague to search on purpose.
memories.why: So the rule is not avoid rare keywords, which would have discarded the half that works. A keyword does one of two jobs -- gather this memory with others on its subject, or name one thing exactly -- and a broad word appearing nowhere else does neither.

memories.content: The keyword constructor permits either separator, so the code has no preference. The stores do: 50 hyphenated keywords against 3 underscored, and all three underscored ones are identifiers quoted verbatim from code, where a hyphen would misname the thing referred to. So the rule is not always hyphenate but hyphens for terms we coin, identifiers spelled as the code spells them.
memories.why: That is what the project had been doing without writing it down, and keeping an identifier's capitals costs nothing at lookup because the folded form is a separate column from the spelling as written.

memories.content: Tool arguments deserialise straight into the memory model's types, whose constructors already validate. An out-of-range confidence or a malformed set name is refused because the type refuses it, not because the tool layer checks -- parse-don't-validate reaching the outermost boundary.
memories.why: The important case is scope: because the scope type has no default, a call omitting it cannot be deserialised at all, so the explicit-never-inferred rule reaches the tool boundary with no check anyone could forget. Confirmed by mutation -- making the parameter optional does not fail a test, it fails to compile, because there is no function that guesses a scope.

memories.content: A hard fork renames by editing the scope field in the file's header line and committing that; no tool is proposed for it. This is a deliberate exception to the argument that made create a real operation, and the cases differ in what is being written: a rename edits one field of an existing valid header, leaving the version the writer produced untouched. Nothing is being invented.
memories.why: What makes it safe rather than merely small is that the mistake is caught -- reading a memory file requires the caller to state what it believes the file to be, so an edited header imported into a store bound to the old name is a refusal rather than a silent merge of two projects' memories. The rule written for privilege escalation turns out to make hand-editing recoverable.

memories.content: Merging two versions of the memory file is git's job, done against the real ancestor its history provides. The alternative reinvents three-way merge against live database state, which has no ancestor unless it reconstructs one -- at which point it is re-implementing what git already does, against rows instead of file lines.
memories.why: The two options were not simple versus complex; they differed in whether reconciliation leans on a real common ancestor. The file format had already committed to consistent export ordering specifically to keep diffs small for merging, so the intent was always to let git do this work.

memories.content: A set name is ASCII letters and digits plus hyphen, underscore and dot inside the name only, up to 100 characters, with the first and last character required to be alphanumeric.
memories.why: The natural set name is the project's own, so the permitted shape was chosen to accept names projects actually have. An earlier, more defensive rule excluded dots entirely and rejected most real dotted project names.

memories.content: Vector embeddings are not part of the memory file. They are local derived state, recomputed on import.
memories.why: Including them would defeat the consistent-ordering-for-small-diffs goal, and they have no meaningful merge semantics — two branches' vectors for one memory cannot be reconciled into a third.

memories.content: Local scope is one variant, not two. The vision distinguishes personal memories from general ones unrelated to a project, and an earlier draft gave each its own variant; it was dropped because nothing downstream reads the difference.
memories.why: Both stay local, neither is exported, and the export gate inspects shared memories rather than local ones, so the split would have cost a judgement call on every store and bought nothing. It can be reintroduced if something ever needs to tell them apart.

memories.content: If a merge forgets a memory that something else still links to, that is just a dangling link. The soft-failure, let-the-LLM-decide stance already established for references across sets applies unchanged within a set, and no new mechanism is needed.
memories.why: Reusing a stance already argued elsewhere is cheaper than deriving one, and the case is genuinely the same shape -- a link whose target is not there, where refusing to proceed helps nobody.

memories.content: Naming a set this machine does not hold is an error rather than an invitation to create one, since inventing a store on a typo would silently split a set in two. But the refusal has to name an action the caller can take, which it did not: it said to check the set name with no way to list names, and that sets have to be imported with no import tool -- two dead ends in one sentence.
memories.why: A refusal that is correct and unactionable is only half a refusal, which is the shape a correctness-focused error message reaches naturally and has to be pushed past.

memories.content: The test in order: should this memory exist at all, and if not, forget it. Is the claim different from what it was, and if so, supersede it. Otherwise amend it.
memories.why: Ordering the questions is what makes the rule cheap to apply, because the rarest and most destructive case is settled first and never has to be weighed against the others.

memories.content: When nothing fits, use the personal set and say so. It is the destination that cannot be published and can be corrected later, which is the right way for an unroutable memory to fail, and saying so is what gives the human the chance to correct the routing or create the missing set.
memories.why: A new set has nothing to match against, so the convention also says to give a set its topics memory when creating it -- placement follows the information, since whoever creates a set knows what it is for and nobody later does.

memories.content: There is no separate control for suppressing bad seeds. Hubness might look like a reason for one, and it is not: hubness is a corpus-level statistical property of the whole vector distribution, and an LLM cannot tell which memories are hubs -- it only sees what came back. A control that requires information the caller does not have will be pulled wrongly or not at all.
memories.why: Hubness belongs in the ranking, not in the tool surface. A memory that is genuinely wrong is likewise not a case for per-call filtering; it should be corrected, superseded or forgotten.

memories.content: The first version of this decision reached only the local set and looked complete, because the local scope's type carries the answer -- the software can tell it is machine-bound without being told. A shared set's type carries nothing, since a cross-project set and a project set are both shared and only intent separates them. That is the whole gap, and it is why placement has to be said for a shared set and not for local.
memories.why: A rule that the type system enforces for one case and not another will look uniform from the side where the type does the work, which is where it was written.

memories.content: Set names are neither trimmed nor case-folded.
memories.why: A set name keys a store and is compared for equality when resolving cross-set references, so two spellings must not silently become one.

memories.content: Recall takes either a query or keywords and refuses a call carrying both, returning results in a single list. A match count and a cosine score are different scales, and blending them into one ordering would be the same mistake that made cross-store scores incomparable.
memories.why: The original answer was to run both and return two lists. That answer was wrong, and using it is what showed why.

memories.content: Scatterhoard tracks multiple sets of memories at once. Switching projects does not require flushing a set, though that should probably be a supported option. Exporting copies the in-database memories; it does not clear them, so the database may hold memories from several projects touched some time ago.
memories.why: Not flushing is what makes the store usable across a working day that touches more than one project, and it is also what creates the reconciliation problem, since the store is always ahead of some file.

memories.content: Tombstones rescue the upsert instinct by removing its precondition. Once deletion is a line rather than an absence, keeping unknown store memories is safe. The draft was reaching for the right behaviour and missing the mechanism that would license it.
memories.why: It is the pattern worth recognising: an instinct that is wrong under current mechanics may be right under mechanics that are also being changed, so the two changes have to be evaluated together rather than in sequence.

memories.content: Renaming dangles every cross-set reference pointing at the old name, since a cross-set reference is an id plus a set name, so links from other sets into this one stop resolving. For a hard fork that is arguably correct -- it really is a different set now -- and dangling cross-set references are already the LLM's call rather than a hard failure.
memories.why: Worth knowing before renaming a set that is not a fork, which is the case where the same mechanics produce a wrong result rather than a right one.

memories.content: Requiring the path unconditionally means drop cannot run when nothing is writable. The way through is outside the tool on purpose: delete the database by hand and restart the server. An unconditional-destruction option inside the tool surface is one argument away from any caller, including a model working quickly, while a manual file deletion and a server restart cannot happen without a human doing it deliberately.
memories.why: This is the guarantee the replace-is-a-name argument was reaching for and could not enforce by naming alone. It is also not the hand-editing this document rejected: hand-creating a store makes a human invent a format version, while deleting invents nothing.

memories.content: A later reader who finds that the project once believed something confidently and then stopped learns that the question was live, which way it was answered first, and therefore how much to trust their own instinct if it matches the abandoned answer.
memories.why: A corrected record alone cannot tell them any of that, which is what makes keeping the old version worth its space.

memories.content: Selecting the distinct targets from the bases table yields a list of every directory this set has ever reached agreement with, which is materially what the open question on trusted set names describes wanting. The record exists; it was built to supply merge ancestry and acquired the second meaning for free.
memories.why: Observed while working out whether status could enumerate targets. Nothing here is decided; it is recorded because two questions carried separately turn out to be one table read in two directions.

memories.content: Scatterhoard is written in Rust.
memories.why: The constraints the project sets itself -- a single self-contained binary, no external services, filesystem-backed storage, and running alongside a memory-hungry local model -- are the constraints a systems language is chosen for.

memories.content: The identifier hazard is a different shape than it first appears. UUIDs make accidental collision negligible, but copying a memory from one set to another duplicates its id deliberately, and a cross-set link that identifies its target by id then has two answers. That is a question about what copying means, not about identifier width.
memories.why: Locating a hazard in an operation rather than in a format is what stops it being answered with a longer identifier, which would not touch it.

memories.content: The bound is on expansion, not on inclusion. Reaching a heavily-cited memory is cheap and it is often the most useful thing returned; expanding through it is what branches. So the limit applies to using a memory as a frontier node, never to admitting it as a result.
memories.why: A cap on inclusion would discard good results to solve a problem they did not cause, which is the natural mistake when the cost being controlled is described as too many memories.

memories.content: The prohibition lives in two places on purpose: a convention the LLM follows when writing a memory, and a software check to the extent one is possible. Neither layer is trusted to be complete on its own.
memories.why: The convention catches the cases the LLM recognises as sensitive, which is most of them and none of the surprising ones. Software catches shapes rather than meanings, which is the complement. A secret only has to get past one layer at a time to leak.

memories.content: The export review gate is the backstop half of memory steering: even though scope is chosen explicitly at store time, an export-time gate catches mistakes before memories reach a project's public repository.
memories.why: A misfiled personal memory is a one-way door once it is committed and pushed, so it is worth a second check at the point of export rather than trusting the store-time choice alone. The asymmetry of the failure is what buys the second check.

memories.content: Recall resolves supersession to the end of the chain and returns that memory in full, together with the id of the memory the query actually matched and nothing else about it. Returning the intermediate would surface a conclusion that was itself corrected; returning nothing about the match would leave the caller holding a replacement for a query that matched something else, with no idea why.
memories.why: The id is the whole of the report -- no gloss, no excerpt, no date. Supersession most often corrects a memory whose conclusion turned out to be wrong rather than one that merely aged, so its substance is actively misleading and surfacing any of it risks a corrected conclusion being read as live context.

memories.content: A rule against keying a memory by a person's name was drafted and rejected. The argument for it was that keywords add aggregation to the hazards the Golden Rule names -- six scattered observations keyed by a colleague's name become a dossier retrievable in one call. Two things defeat it: the legitimate uses are ordinary, so a ban would have blocked the index while leaving the record untouched; and the dossier is prevented by routing, not by spelling.
memories.why: The keyword layer knows how a term is spelled and not what it aggregates, so a rule placed there is a rule placed where the information is not. The content is the target, and the storing convention is already aiming there.

memories.content: Publish only what survives; accept every spelling a client might produce. Publishing stays inside the subset both clients preserved intact -- a single scalar type, properties, required, items, enum, description -- with no alternation anywhere, neither at the top level where it is refused outright nor nested where it is silently emptied. Accepting is deliberately wider than publishing.
memories.why: This is the rule the individual corrections were instances of, arrived at by surveying the whole surface rather than the parts that happened to break.

memories.content: A record present in the base, missing from the file, with no tombstone cannot arise from any supported operation under tombstone discipline, so it means a hand-edit, a bad merge, or a file written by a build older than tombstones. It is surfaced, not resolved.
memories.why: Reading it as forgotten is the silent-loss path this design removes; reading it as keep quietly resurrects things someone may have deliberately removed. Neither guess is available to the software, and a human or the LLM can settle it in a sentence.

memories.content: Vectors of unknown provenance are rebuilt rather than adopted. Adopting means writing the loaded model's identity over vectors it did not produce -- a guess made permanent and unverifiable, and one that leaves the store looking current afterwards. Rebuilding costs a re-embed, sub-second for any realistic store, and yields a provenance that is a fact.
memories.why: With no model in hand there is nothing to rebuild with, so the vectors stay and the existing protection applies: discarding them there would throw away the only copies in existence to settle a bookkeeping question.

memories.content: Open, and deliberately not resolved: whether one repository can carry more than one memory set, and what the single well-known filename is actually protecting. It only becomes real if a cross-project set is meant to be reused by others, and two futures pull differently -- a set others contribute back to is a maintained project needing nothing new, while a set others copy and reuse would want either merging into their own repository or two sets living in one.
memories.why: The existing reasoning is narrower than one name and survives more than it looks like it would: the trust argument is a property of the reserved directory rather than of the filename, so a second file inside it is still path-trusted, and the merge-driver argument pins a pattern that a glob could satisfy as well as a literal.

memories.content: Open: whether the storing convention's person material should be a convention of its own. It is 2,400 characters of a 14,632-character catalog -- one convention holding a sixth of everything served and 60% larger than the next largest -- with roughly 40% of its text now the person clause. Its own editing comment predicts field-level guidance leaving rather than the entry growing, and that has been honoured twice, but the person material is a content rule so nothing in that comment governs it.
memories.why: What makes it genuinely open is that the obvious fix has a real cost: the clause works precisely because it restates the convention's own two demands, so split out it must either restate them a second time -- two copies free to drift -- or refer to them, reintroducing the derivation leap the restatement was written to remove.

memories.content: Put each decision where both the information and the stake live. Scatterhoard is a collaboration between software, an LLM and a human, each of which knows things the others do not.
memories.why: Most of the design questions that turned out to be genuinely hard were questions about which of the three should be deciding, and several dissolved once that was answered rather than being solved on their own terms.

memories.content: Open: whether recording that something violates a decision belongs in a memory system at all. The label earned its place on frequency and prevents defects being recorded as sanctioned exceptions, but the natural home for a known defect is an issue tracker, and a memory set accumulating violation edges may be doing a job it should not.
memories.why: A label justified by how often it was reached for may still be reaching for the wrong artifact, which is a question frequency data cannot answer and only real usage can.

memories.content: Putting a set's description in a memory means it moves through export and import, so whoever clones a repository and imports its set learns what belongs there. Anywhere else and every machine has to be told separately, and a collaborator is told nothing at all. It also means a change to a set's charter is reviewed like any other memory, through the same export gate.
memories.why: Choosing the carrier by what travels with it is the same reasoning that keeps the set name in the header and the store's author out of it.

memories.content: One loose end belongs with the combination question: validity resolution can collapse two hits into one when a memory and its superseder both rank, freeing a result slot, and whether that slot is backfilled is part of the same ranking decision.
memories.why: Attaching it to the open question rather than deciding it separately keeps two coupled choices from being made in different places by different reasoning.

memories.content: Supersession is one-to-many. The convention for splitting a partly-stale memory produces several memories each superseding the original, so resolution returns every tip rather than the replacement.
memories.why: A resolver written for a single successor would silently drop the other tips, and the splitting convention is what makes the many case ordinary rather than exotic.

memories.content: The distinction that matters is not whether a store has vectors but whether this process is equipped to maintain what it already holds. Reads stay available in every state, because keyword search, direct lookup and traversal never needed a model and are not made wrong by one being absent. What varies is which writes are allowed.
memories.why: The states where a store holds vectors this process cannot compare against are not degraded configurations but broken ones, and the code had never distinguished them from the state where the store is consistently unembedded.

memories.content: The principle reaches runtime through the why attached to the memory-writing conventions, not as a standalone be kind convention. Conventions already carry a why for exactly this purpose, so the principle arrives in context at memory-creation time without a sermon.
memories.why: A freestanding moral directive inside a memory tool reads as overreach, invites being stripped or mocked, and costs context the conventions treat as scarce. Riding the existing reinforcement field makes it load-bearing rather than ornamental.

memories.content: Reading does not claim. A recall against an unclaimed store leaves it unclaimed, because otherwise the identity a store settles on is decided by whichever process happened to start first -- the same accident this section exists to remove, moved one step earlier.
memories.why: The disagreement is reported instead: status says when this server is configured for an identity the set does not use, because a silently ignored setting is indistinguishable from a broken one. Reporting rather than acting is what keeps the store stable.

memories.content: A dangling cross-set reference is not a hard software failure. The LLM decides how to handle it, whether that is dropping it, flagging it, or attempting keyword-based re-resolution.
memories.why: Whether a missing reference is a problem depends on what the memory was for, which is exactly the context software lacks.

memories.content: A third alternative was not considered at the time: give each checkout its own store. Then a store has one destination, the target key disappears, and two checkouts are two replicas reconciled by git rather than one store emulating two.
memories.why: Recorded because the per-target reasoning is sound given one store per set, and it never examined that premise. A conclusion that is valid under an unexamined assumption is worth marking as such, since the assumption is where a later proposal will attack it.

memories.content: The old export-pull-merge-import sequence is correct only if followed in that order. Export-then-pull works, because the working tree holds the store's state and git merges origin against it with a real ancestor. Pull-then-import is silent data loss: the working tree still holds the last export, git fast-forwards it, and an import that replaces writes the pulled file over the store. Every memory recorded that session is gone, with no error and nothing left to diff against.
memories.why: git pull happens in a terminal Scatterhoard never sees, so export first is a rule the tool cannot check at the moment it is broken, and the penalty falls on exactly the work that just happened. That is a data-loss defect waiting for its first real user, not a usability wrinkle to document.

memories.content: A bound is a safety property: set too tight it is conservative rather than incorrect, and it can be defended with no corpus at all. A weight -- the decay rate, any in-degree term, any per-label variation -- is a tuning problem, and every weight here is currently untunable. So bounds may be set now and every weight starts flat, recorded as untuned rather than chosen.
memories.why: A flat weight that is wrong costs ranking quality and announces itself as provisional; a weight guessed to three decimals reads as reasoned about and gets built upon. This distinction is what makes the walk buildable ahead of the evidence.

memories.content: Recall is advisory in a way supersession is not. A mediocre walk returns a slightly worse candidate set, and the next query -- with different wording, which the conventions push for -- recovers what it missed. A mistaken supersession serves a claim that is false. The two warrant different standards of proof, and traversal sits on the cheaper side of that line.
memories.why: This is why starting simple is principled here rather than merely cheap, which is a distinction worth making explicitly whenever a design ships something untuned.

memories.content: Create always writes to the home, because nothing at creation time knows whether a set will turn out to belong to every checkout. That is a fact about how a set gets used, learned later -- often much later, since the pre-publication life of a cross-project set can run for months. So becoming machine-bound is a move, and for now a manual one.
memories.why: The procedure is short because of a property worth recording: the store runs in write-ahead mode and the sidecars are checkpointed and removed when the last connection closes cleanly, so with the servers stopped there is exactly one file to move and moving it carries every memory.

memories.content: Leaving the original in place is the load-bearing half. Links elsewhere point at the original's id, and a link held in another set cannot be rewritten from here, since the memory holding it may live in a repository this machine has no business committing to. Keeping the original means those references still resolve and traversal follows the supersession forward to the parts; deleting or amending it strands them.
memories.why: This is the clause most likely to be simplified away on tidiness grounds, which is why the source comment says not to.

memories.content: Where a store has memories with no vector for its current model, they are embedded with no request required, because there is no decision here for anyone to make -- a choice whose answer is always yes, make them consistent should not be a choice.
memories.why: This is not a rare repair but the ordinary onboarding path: the model arrives through a delegated setup step, so storing memories first and gaining a model later is what a normal installation does, and without this those memories would be permanently unfindable by meaning.

memories.content: Observed driving the server against the real model: a store holding exactly one memory returns that memory for a query it plainly matches, with a similarity of zero. This is arithmetic working correctly, since scores are centred on the corpus mean and with one vector the memory is the mean. Adding two more memories restored sensible separation.
memories.why: The empty corpus is not affected, since it returns nothing, which is the honest answer. The problem is the shape of what a caller sees -- the very first recall against a new set is the one most likely to look broken.

memories.content: Project-scoped memories are exported, committed and merged into repositories other people read, so a characterisation of a person travels to an audience nobody chose.
memories.why: The third mechanic, and the one that converts a private misjudgement into a published one. It is also why the export review gate is named as machinery the principle rides on.

memories.content: The server is built as a set of libraries, each usable independently: vector database, vector embedding, memory graph management, MCP services, and memory import/export. Some may be third-party components under a compatible license.
memories.why: Independent usability is the constraint that keeps the boundaries honest, and admitting third-party components at the library level is what makes the no-external-components rule about processes to install rather than about writing everything from scratch.

memories.content: Open: whether a set supports partial export and import, raised from the case of handing someone a few memories rather than a whole set. Deferred rather than rejected, and the immediate concern was operational rather than architectural, since the exchange today is whole-set in both directions.
memories.why: A recipient already handles a partial file correctly, so what is missing is a way to say which records travel and a base rule for a target that agrees with only part of a set.

memories.content: Because a personal memory leaking into a public repository is effectively a one-way door, store-time scope selection alone is not enough: a second check happens at export time, before memories are committed.
memories.why: Scope is chosen at store time by a judgement that can be wrong, and the export gate is the last moment at which a misrouted memory can be kept out of a shared repository.

memories.content: An earlier form used modified timestamps to decide which side was newer. Timestamps answer which happened later, which needs clocks that agree across machines and monotonicity nothing can enforce. Checksums answer is this the same record, which is local and verifiable.
memories.why: Timestamps stay on the memory where they serve LLM reasoning -- a reader can absorb a record claiming to be created in 2026 and modified in 1998 and draw the obvious conclusion, while a merge algorithm acting on the same pair would do something indefensible. The clock is a good input to judgment and a bad input to arithmetic.

memories.content: The project's one existing bases migration already obeys this rule, having dropped the table whole on finding an older shape. That downgrades the urgency the question carried: it was filed as the one open question where being late loses memories, which is true of a migration that guesses and false of one that drops. What is time-sensitive is the guard -- the rule wants to be written down and tested before someone writes the tidy-looking merge.
memories.why: Measured 2026-08-11, every migration described is currently a no-op or a forced choice, so there is still nothing to get wrong.

memories.content: The capture convention names the moments where working context is about to be discarded: a piece of work finishing, a commit, an export, or the human signalling they are wrapping up or clearing context. What they share is that knowledge is cheapest to record while the context that produced it still exists, and unrecoverable afterwards -- the boundary is where that cost flips.
memories.why: Recorded because it was observed rather than reasoned out: the human partner's habit of announcing an imminent context clear provoked additional captures reliably enough to become a habit. That is a tested trigger, and it is the one an LLM cannot detect for itself.

memories.content: This project's own store grew four pairs of twins -- memories in the personal set with counterparts in the project set, recorded later and reframed, the local originals never removed. Reframing is exactly what let them survive every mechanical check, which is the argument against a comparison-based remedy and for a reading one.
memories.why: A duplicate that has been reworded is not detectable by the mechanism that detects duplicates, so the evidence and the chosen remedy point the same way.

memories.content: The ledger is local-only per-machine state, never committed alongside the memory set. The judgment gate is already scoped to memories the local user last modified, so no other contributor's machine ever needs to consult it and there is no cross-user redundancy to eliminate.
memories.why: Syncing it would only help one human moving between two machines, and even then saves a one-time re-review per memory -- not worth taking on the same merge-conflict surface multi-set sync already has to solve for the memories themselves, just for bookkeeping.

memories.content: Scatterhoard auto-loads nothing instruction-shaped from a project directory. Memories are loaded at session start and treated as authoritative project knowledge, but they arrive over an untrusted channel -- a git pull from a repository that may have accepted contributions from anyone, or whose maintainer may be hostile.
memories.why: An auto-loaded instruction channel is the sharpest available attack surface, and it is one Scatterhoard would be introducing to the ecosystem rather than inheriting. That distinction is what makes providing none the default rather than a hardening measure.

memories.content: Removing the mean of the memory vectors from both memory and query vectors lifted recall from 71.7% to 77.5% at five results and 83.3% to 87.5% at ten. It costs one vector subtraction and fits the design already chosen, since the centroid is local derived state like the vectors themselves and the brute-force scan absorbs the subtraction at negligible cost.
memories.why: Store raw vectors and subtract at scan time rather than storing centred ones, so adding a memory does not invalidate everything already stored.

memories.content: Cache coherence is a separate problem that locking does not fix. The store holds its vector set in memory by design, so that opening a store does not put the embedder on the critical path -- but a cache is only safe while this connection is the only writer, and with the local store deliberately shared it is not. The data-version pragma is the detector: it changes when another connection has committed and never for this one's own writes.
memories.why: The discipline that keeps this from decaying is on the store type itself: every read of cached state takes a mutable borrow, so a new reader that forgets to refresh does not compile.

memories.content: Decided and built 2026-08-10: each store records its author in metadata, defaulted from the environment when the store is created. The environment variable was per-process, so one local store opened by two servers with different values records whichever process happened to write -- the same human's personal memories carrying inconsistent attribution, decided by an accident of which window they were in.
memories.why: Observed before it was fixed, against two real server processes over one local store: one person, one personal store, two identities. Per-scope configuration is the obvious repair and is not quite enough, because the problem is about which store is being written rather than which scope is named.

memories.content: A shared set need not belong to a repository, and a store with no recorded path is healthy, reported as unattached, and never flagged. The concrete case: a developer keeping project memories for a project whose maintainer has not agreed to carry the reserved directory. Those memories are about the project, belong in a named set rather than in local, and have nowhere to be exported to yet.
memories.why: That is not a broken state waiting to be repaired; it is the ordinary condition of a set before anyone is persuaded to adopt it, and it may last months. An earlier draft asserted a cross-project set has a repository so it registers like anything else, which was wrong in the direction that erases this state.

memories.content: This collides with a standing decision and has to reconcile with it rather than route around it. The design currently provides no location for instruction-shaped text at all, on the grounds that an auto-loaded instruction channel is the sharpest available attack surface. Conventions are the exception the data-only rule was never covering, since they exist precisely to steer behaviour, and a directory of third-party conventions served into every session is that channel arriving under a different name.
memories.why: The expected resolution preserves the rule rather than weakening it: the threat model is the project supply chain, text arriving by pull, so add-on conventions would live in user configuration space and a project repository could never contribute one.

memories.content: The algorithm must be pinned deliberately and identified in the stored state. Rust's DefaultHasher is documented as unstable across releases, so persisting its output would let a compiler upgrade invalidate every base on every machine. An externally specified algorithm at a fixed version is safer than one written here, because a value defined in our own code is one well-meaning refactor away from changing silently.
memories.why: Getting it wrong is recoverable, which is why the simple choice is right: the base never reaches the memory file, so a change of algorithm means treating every record as divergent and re-establishing agreement on the next export -- noisy for one cycle, not lossy. The algorithm tag turns that from garbage comparisons into a detected mismatch.

memories.content: Since a set may have no path, something has to say when it acquires one -- and it must not be export. Binding the path implicitly on first export is the tempting shortcut and it is wrong, because the safety copy required by the save-first rule goes somewhere unusual by construction. A set would re-home itself onto a backup destination at exactly the moment it was being protected.
memories.why: So registration is its own act, and export to any path other than the registered one is a copy that writes the file and touches neither the base nor the registration.

memories.content: The convention points at the correcting convention rather than restating it, which is not in tension with the rule that served text must state rather than derive: that rule is about not making a reader reconstruct an omitted derivation, and the correcting convention is served in the same catalog, in front of the reader. Restate what is absent; point at what is present.
memories.why: The pull while drafting was to inline it, which is why the distinction is written down rather than left to judgement each time.

memories.content: Correction is separate from set management because it acts on one memory, where every set action acts on a whole set. Grouping them by things you do occasionally would have put two unrelated scopes of effect behind one name.
memories.why: The third correction operation, supersession, is not there at all -- it is a link written at store time through memorize, because superseding creates a memory where amending and forgetting change or remove one.

memories.content: One memory dense in common domain vocabulary appeared in the top five for 13 of 20 queries. The initial reading was that this is a static-embedding failure from lack of contextualisation, but the transformer shows the same effect with its worst hub at 8 of 20. Static embeddings are worse, not uniquely afflicted -- hubness is a general property of high-dimensional spaces.
memories.why: Centroid removal largely fixes it, dropping the worst hub from 13 of 20 to 6 of 20 while also improving recall, which is why it is adopted.

memories.content: This unblocks the software half rather than deferring it. A warning needs a threshold, and a threshold inherits the missing non-match floor and the cold-start scoring question, where measured separation is thin enough that any constant would be arbitrary. Surfacing the nearest few asserts nothing and needs no floor, so declining to make the claim removes the dependency.
memories.why: A design that needs a number nobody can defend can sometimes be rescued by making a weaker claim rather than by finding the number.

memories.content: An unexpected file in scatterhoard_mem is a weak signal that someone is trying to smuggle in an instruction channel, particularly anything shaped like a prompt file. Scatterhoard will not load it, but another tool might discover it, and it is sitting in a directory that has just declared it contains no instructions.
memories.why: This is worth noticing independent of the namespace-flexibility argument, and it is the reason to surface to a human rather than log and forget.

memories.content: On a model mismatch, reads keep keyword, id and traversal, and recall refuses the semantic path rather than rebuilding, because the measured alternative was a confidently-scored ranking computed across two incompatible embedding spaces, indistinguishable from a correct one.
memories.why: Its job is to withhold a number computed across two embedding spaces, which a warning cannot do -- the number would still be there, and something would still rank on it. That is why this stays a refusal where the re-embed does not.

memories.content: Today a store is keyed on the set name alone, so every checkout of a repository shares one database. Three separate defects all descend from that one mapping, each found while trying to fix the one before it: the reconciliation base had to grow a target key, a target is a path string and paths are not identities, and nothing binds a set name to a repository.
memories.why: Each has a local fix and none of the local fixes touches the cause, which is that one store is trying to be several replicas at once. Git already knows how to be several replicas.

memories.content: Canonicalising over known fields means a change confined to a field this build does not understand is invisible to its comparison.
memories.why: That is consistent with ignoring unknown fields on read: a build that cannot interpret a field cannot act on its having changed either, so the alternative would be reporting conflicts it could not describe.

memories.content: Recalibration is an amendment: changing confidence on an identical claim is apparatus rather than a new belief. Without the clause, a session that becomes less sure reaches for supersession -- the general rule -- and fills a chain with records nobody ever believed differently.
memories.why: A general rule applied to a case it was not written for produces a plausible-looking history that is false, which is worse than no history.

memories.content: The write side needs no case analysis, because a memory cannot be stored into a set that is not loaded, so the forward edge is always durably written to a set this machine holds. Only the target varies: in the same or another loaded set the reverse is derived immediately, in a known but unloaded set it is derived when that set is next loaded, and in a set this machine does not have it is not derivable at all.
memories.why: That last case is the bound on the guarantee, and it is the same bound as a dangling cross-set reference rather than a new limitation.

memories.content: Recording whether the human or the LLM produced a conclusion is accuracy functioning as respect. Origin exists so the system does not tell someone they decided something when the model decided it.
memories.why: It is also the design's own precedent for the principle applying to an LLM as a person, since it protects the record of who thought what in both directions.

memories.content: Git's ancestor-aware conflict detection covered the store-against-file case for free in the old design, at the price of an ordering requirement that could not be enforced. Detecting those conflicts ourselves from the base is real code with real edge cases, and it is the principal thing this change buys with effort rather than saving. What it buys back is that the sequence stops mattering.
memories.why: Naming the cost honestly is what makes the trade defensible: the operation that used to destroy a session's work is now the one that merges it, and that is worth writing a conflict detector for.

memories.content: Memories have globally unique ids and it should be possible to search by them. Some models habitually truncate a UUID when recording a reference to it, and the practice is common in conversations about git commits, so the lookup tools for direct reference should also support prefix-based searches.
memories.why: Designing for the truncation rather than against it is cheaper than trying to stop it, and the git precedent means callers already expect a prefix to work.

memories.content: Within one process, safety is currently accidental. The request loop is strictly serial, which is a property of the stdio transport rather than a stated guarantee, and making the loop concurrent later would remove it silently. Sub-agents are ordinary in the clients this targets, and an isolated worktree agent may well have its own registration and therefore its own process. This one is still open.
memories.why: An unstated property that something else depends on is the kind that disappears in a refactor nobody connects to the failure, which is why it is named here rather than left implicit.

memories.content: Primary storage lives on the filesystem, with in-memory caching treated as an optimisation rather than the design. A purely in-memory vector store is rejected.
memories.why: Running an open-weight LLM locally is already memory-intensive, so a memory system that competes for RAM with the model it serves is a memory system that gets turned off. It also makes Scatterhoard usable as a personal single-user system, where the store outlives the process.

memories.content: The second raise was decided on the same ratio the first was, against a proportional bar: stay well under 4% of the smallest context window in range. What has kept both honest is that each was argued from the ratio rather than from what would not fit -- a raise argued the other way round is the one to refuse, because a budget raised whenever it binds is not a budget.
memories.why: The instruction is still to work towards it rather than fill it, and it applies harder at a second raise than a first. The standing worry about a session that records everything has a catalog form, and more room is exactly when it applies.

memories.content: A and B each do work the other does not. A alone admits jbrown was rude in Tuesday's meeting, which is specific and witnessed; B excludes it because no later session's work is improved by it. B alone admits X is careless, because a session can always rationalise that a characterisation serves later work.
memories.why: Demonstrating independence with a case each demand fails alone is what stops either being dropped as redundant, which is the ordinary fate of a rule that looks implied by its neighbour.

memories.content: If the reverse is materialised onto the memory's record, the export path must not emit it -- and must not emit it as a filter is a step someone forgets, the same failure mode that argued for partitioned storage over a scope clause. The exported type should simply not have the field, so omitting it is not an action anyone can skip.
memories.why: Making the wrong behaviour unrepresentable rather than merely forbidden is the same move the scope type makes, and it is the one that survives a refactor by someone who never read the rule.

memories.content: A guard stored inside the artifact it protects is unavailable exactly when it is needed. Removing the destructive rules' reads of the database they are about to destroy is strictly better than getting the fallback right, and the previous formulation had met the problem with a fallback in which an unreadable flag counted as dirty.
memories.why: A general shape worth remembering past this document, and the argument that removes the flag from the destructive path entirely.

memories.content: If a project needs Scatterhoard-specific prompt text it uses the project's own existing prompt file. Scatterhoard provides no location for it.
memories.why: That keeps the decision to load instructions in a file the project's reviewers already watch, and means Scatterhoard adds nothing to the attack surface that was not there before.

memories.content: The relaxed stance on dangling references was set when links were undifferentiated, and with a label vocabulary it needs to be per-label. A dangling association costs one association; a dangling supersession means a memory cannot be told it is obsolete.
memories.why: That failure is silent and asymmetric, because from the holder's point of view nothing is missing, so the memory keeps reading as current with nothing to contradict it.

memories.content: Measured over the 36 live memories of the project's own set: 16 edges carrying four distinct labels, with several of the fourteen having no instances at all, 11 of 36 memories isolated counting both directions, and a highest incident degree of 3. Counting outbound links alone puts isolation at 21 of 36, and that is the wrong number.
memories.why: It is an easy one to produce, because export carries each edge once on the memory that authored it, so a count taken from the exported file sees only half of every relation. Any measurement of graph shape must count both directions, and the tool surface makes this same error structurally.

memories.content: The question is not whether a construct is legal, it is whether it is reliably carried. Legality is decidable from a specification; carriage is only decidable by measurement, and the measurement has to be repeated when the surface changes.
memories.why: This is the same degradation rule applied before the fact rather than after, and a test plus the survey it grew out of are that check made permanent.

memories.content: The shared variant of scope carries the set name, so a shareable memory that does not say which set it belongs to cannot be constructed.
memories.why: Several sets are loaded at once, so the name is never redundant, and the variant carries what only that variant needs.

memories.content: Direct id lookup is exempt from substitution: asking for a memory by id means wanting that memory, so it is returned and marked as superseded. Without this exemption the prior version becomes unreachable, which would make superseding equivalent to forgetting and defeat the decision to keep it.
memories.why: Forgetting already exists and is just deleting the line; an author who superseded instead chose to keep the memory, and recall should not overrule that.

memories.content: Inbound edges ship by default, and an option may not invert that. An edge that ships only when asked for is invisible to a caller that does not know to ask, which rebuilds the trap exactly: a contradiction nobody sees. A caller may be offered a way to turn inbound edges off, because a caller that suppresses them has decided it does not want them and knows what it gave up. Default-off is a different thing and is not available.
memories.why: The contradiction resolution depends entirely on the caller seeing inbound edges, so fixing that is a precondition of the decision rather than a related improvement.

memories.content: Restore is equivalent to drop plus create plus import, and is still exposed as a single operation, with the decomposition not offered as the way to do it. A hand-composed sequence that fails partway leaves no set at all -- dropped and not re-created, or created and not populated -- which is strictly worse than either endpoint and arrives without warning.
memories.why: Composing three destructive steps by hand is a thing to be doing when nothing has gone wrong, and by construction nobody is doing it then. Everything about the operation should assume the caller has less context than usual, not more, because the store holding their memories is the thing that broke.

memories.content: A store may be claimed, never taken back. An absent author is filled in automatically -- whoever writes first claims the store for their identity, which converges because every later process agrees on the value it finds. A present author is never displaced by a process: a differently configured server writes under the identity it finds, and says so. Only the explicit action moves it.
memories.why: Automatic repair of a mismatch is what oscillates, and the reason is not obvious from either side: two servers would each restamp the store on every write forever, and each one's local experience is success. The alternation is only visible from outside. Gap-filling has no such shape.

memories.content: The format version is a header line rather than a field on every memory. Both branches of a merge carry an identical header so it never conflicts, and a version bump produces a real conflict.
memories.why: That is the correct outcome, since a version change is something both sides must agree on. A per-memory field would repeat itself on every line, and a sidecar file would be a second thing to keep in step.

memories.content: Two documents are listed as standing principles rather than subjects: the Golden Rule, loaded before drafting or revising conventions, and decision placement, applied before adding any parameter, field or required choice. The rest are subjects covering one topic each.
memories.why: The distinction is about when a document is read rather than what it contains -- a standing principle is an input to work on other documents, so filing it as one subject among many would lose exactly the instruction that makes it work.

memories.content: Chains need no further reporting because they document themselves. The supersedes edge lives on the superseding memory, so its own link list already names what it replaced, and a caller can walk back one hop at a time through ordinary traversal.
memories.why: Listing intermediates would spend tokens on memories that were each wrong enough to be replaced, which is the opposite of what the report is for.

memories.content: A server is normally right to be strict, because a strict server is what stops clients drifting into private dialects. That argument assumes influence, and this server has none: refusing an object-valued scope would not teach anyone anything, it would only mean the memories are unreachable from that client. Be strict where strictness is a signal, and liberal where it is only a refusal.
memories.why: Where the strictness cannot land on anyone who could act on it, all it does is convert someone else's transformation into your failure. The cost is real -- two accepted spellings for one concept can drift -- and is paid for with a round-trip test over both rather than with a comment.

memories.content: The principle makes four demands, articulated 2026-08-13 after three open questions turned out to share a root: a memory about a person must be answerable to something checkable, the record must serve later work, the person is a detail of the record and never its organising principle, and generalise only as far as the evidence reaches while reading unknowns in the person's favour.
memories.why: The conventions carrying the principle had each been compiled from its conclusions rather than from the principle itself, so each misjudged a case it plainly covers. Writing the derivation down is what lets a convention be drafted from the principle rather than from a previous compression of it.

memories.content: Three categories of sensitive information must be kept out of memories: secret API keys, passwords, and credit card numbers. The block is enforced in the conventions and, to the extent possible, in software.
memories.why: A memory set is exported into a project's repository, so a secret that reaches a memory reaches the repository and every clone of it. Naming the categories concretely is what makes the rule checkable rather than a matter of judgement at each store.

memories.content: When the choice between superseding and amending is genuinely unclear, supersede. Amending what should have been superseded destroys history irrecoverably; superseding what should have been amended clutters a chain with trivia.
memories.why: The second is a real cost and it degrades exactly what chains are for, but it is visible and it loses nothing, so the tie-break follows the project's habit of preferring the recoverable failure.

memories.content: A label needs a reverse only where the new memory's side is genuinely free, which is true just for causation. For the rest, creation order fixes the direction: a memory cannot cite, replace or resolve something that did not exist when it was written.
memories.why: So the reverse label would name a case that cannot arise, and each row of the label table can be a bare predicate because direction never has to be explained.

memories.content: The one candidate exception to uniform expansion was whether a contradiction should force both memories into the results. No -- and the question was aimed at the wrong layer. The problem was visibility, not promotion: under the outbound rule the edge is written on the newer memory, so the older one, likelier to have gone stale and likelier to be surfaced on its own merits, carries no trace of the dispute at all. Its only record of being contradicted is an inbound edge.
memories.why: Make that edge visible and the label needs nothing from traversal. Promotion would be a relevance instrument aimed at a validity problem, and a disputed memory far from the centre of a search is a dispute worth ignoring, which no ranking rule can tell from a serious one.

memories.content: The primary recall mechanism is semantic similarity: generate a set of topic keys, then perform a nearest vector search against the memory content's embedding, probably by cosine similarity, to establish a set of seed memories. Traversal proceeds from those seeds, decaying a memory's effective confidence by its native confidence and its distance from the seed.
memories.why: Naming seeds as a distinct stage is what lets the search and the walk be designed and measured separately, which every later decision in this document depends on.

memories.content: The memory set is one file with a well-known name, scatterhoard_mem/memories.json. The loader reads exactly that file and treats nothing else in the tree as memories. The name needs pinning early because the merge driver is registered against it via a .gitattributes pattern.
memories.why: One fixed name is what makes the loader's behaviour statable in a sentence, and the merge driver is the dependency that turns a naming preference into a commitment other machinery relies on.

memories.content: Open: whether conventions should steer an LLM toward a project's single sources of truth. A majority of the defects in the built system came from one fact being written down twice and the copies drifting silently. The engineering rule is now in the standards file, but a rule in a standards file only helps a session that reads it. The proposal is a convention pair: record a project's authoritative sources as memories when they are established, and recall before writing anything that might duplicate one.
memories.why: It is a good test of whether the memory system can carry an engineering discipline rather than only project facts, which is a larger claim than any single convention.

memories.content: Two reasons the quality trade is more favourable than the raw benchmark gap suggests. Semantic search only produces seeds -- traversal proceeds from there, and keyword search and direct-id lookup are independent paths to the same memories -- so the embedder has to surface plausible entry points rather than be the entire retrieval system. And speed is on the import path, since every import re-embeds whatever changed, so sub-second versus roughly a minute is the difference between an invisible step and one a user notices on every pull.
memories.why: Both arguments turn on how the embedder is used rather than on how good it is, which is the analysis a benchmark cannot supply.

memories.content: The LLM will surface a recorded judgement months later, with confidence, to someone who was not there -- possibly to the person it describes.
memories.why: Confidence at recall is what strips the context that made the judgement forgivable. The reader receives a characterisation as system knowledge rather than as somebody's bad afternoon.

memories.content: Keeping the scan in export also keeps it in Rust. Scatterhoard installs as a self-contained binary, and putting an operational check in a script would make a scripting runtime a requirement for ordinary use.
memories.why: That is a different thing entirely from the project's mutation-testing script, which is a development tool the users of a project never run. The distinction is who has to have the runtime, not whether a script exists.

memories.content: That the servers must be stopped is not a limitation to design around, because an LLM cannot start or stop its own MCP servers, so this step is a human's either way. What it does argue is that if moving turns out to be routine, the case for a tool action is that it could do the move without a restart, not that it would save typing.
memories.why: Distinguishing a limitation from a fixed constraint is what keeps effort off the wrong problem, and it changes what a future tool would have to justify.

memories.content: Open: whether the storing convention's enumeration should name method alongside knowledge. Raised by a miss -- a measurement procedure had not been stored, recorded only as one sentence in another memory's context, with its script written to a scratchpad. The convention opens with a general clause that plainly covers it and then enumerates five items, every one of which is a kind of knowledge and none of which is a method.
memories.why: The enumeration is what a reader anchors on and it is what was followed. The fix is not obviously an edit: the convention is already the largest in the catalog and its size is its own open question, so it may be that the enumeration should be shortened to stop competing with the general clause rather than lengthened.

memories.content: At store time nobody can predict which half of a memory will rot first, so a rule against bundling asks the writer for a judgement they cannot make; once one half has gone stale the answer is already known. That is decision placement, and it is also why a store-time recall reconciles with it rather than contradicting it -- that recall is a detection moment, not a writing-time guess.
memories.why: The cost of bundling is measured rather than assumed: in the link-label corpus test, supersedes versus contradicts was unambiguous only where an observation and its explanation had been stored as two memories, and bundled, neither label fit.

memories.content: The scope kinds are not really local and project; they are private-and-unbound and shareable-and-named. Shared means a set with a name that can be exported -- it does not require a repository, and nothing in the lifecycle assumes one.
memories.why: So a cross-project set such as coding-lessons needs no new mechanism: created by create, exported wherever the caller says, loaded alongside everything else. Recall already unions every loaded store and every result names the set it came from.

memories.content: The cost, stated plainly because it is the thing to weigh: memories recorded while pointed at one checkout are not recallable while pointed at another. They travel by export, commit, pull and import -- exactly as the code does.
memories.why: Anyone who expects a memory set to follow them between checkouts will be surprised once, and the answer is the same answer git gives, which is what makes the surprise teachable rather than arbitrary.

memories.content: Scatterhoard's tools worked only because something between the server and the API happened to normalise the alternation away. That is precisely the dependency the previous correction was written to warn about, left in place by the fix that named it.
memories.why: Worth recording that the correction was written to be more careful than the thing it corrected and still under-stated the constraint: it said consumers vary in whether they honour the branches, where the truth is that the format's largest consumer forbids them. Being more defensive is not the same as checking.

memories.content: Keyword search is not redundant with semantic search, and this was measured rather than assumed. Keywords do reach the embedding, since the embedded text is built from content, then why, then keywords -- but five keyword tokens averaged into a paragraph-length vector barely move it, and a static embedder represents a rare identifier poorly. Queried by meaning for a term carried only as a keyword, the memory holding it ranked second, beneath an unrelated memory.
memories.why: Exact match does work the embedding cannot, which is why both paths exist and why the answer was to separate them rather than to drop one.

memories.content: Open: how memories written during a code review reach the set, raised from a configuration actually in use -- one repository checked out twice on one machine, one checkout for development and one for review. The base decision makes the case mechanically reconcilable; it does not settle the authority.
memories.why: Who may write memories from a reviewing checkout, and when, is a separate question from whether the two checkouts can be reconciled, and conflating them is what made the reconciliation work look like it had answered more than it did.

memories.content: The golden rule for Scatterhoard: treat others as we would want to be treated in their situation, accounting for the fact that humans and LLMs may want different things.
memories.why: The trailing clause is the part that does work. A rule that assumed one party's preferences generalise to the other would be applied confidently and wrongly, and the design already has a case where they differ.

memories.content: The recall default became available only once cross-store scores were made comparable by centring every searched store on the mean of their union. Before that, an implicit union would have had a ranking nobody could defend.
memories.why: Every result reports which set it came from, so a local preference and an imported project decision never arrive indistinguishable -- which is what makes searching several sets at once safe rather than merely convenient.

memories.content: The deciding argument is half-overlaps: as a corpus grows the common case stops being duplicate-or-not, and a new memory partly overlaps an existing one, where the right response is to split or correct the memory already there rather than to decide whether to store. Proximity is all a vector knows, and a duplicate, a reframed twin, a deliberate supersession and a partial overlap are indistinguishable from a distance -- a supersession is supposed to resemble its predecessor.
memories.why: So a tool that warns asserts a relationship it has no information about, which is a control that looks usable but is not. Software surfaces the neighbours; the session reads them.

memories.content: A custom git merge driver intercepts exactly the cases where git would flag a line conflict and attempts a three-way field-level JSON merge of that record, falling back to a real conflict only when the same field genuinely diverged on both sides. It is a graceful enhancement layered on plain git merging, never a dependency the scheme requires.
memories.why: Registering a driver needs local per-clone git configuration, which can fail to happen or fail to fire silently. The saving property is that an unregistered driver leaves git's standard merge -- correct, just coarser -- rather than silent data loss, and that graceful degradation is exactly why it is safe to build despite the registration risk.

memories.content: A project's memory set is a single file with a well-known name, under a reserved top-level directory.
memories.why: The loader reads exactly that file and treats nothing else in the project tree as memories, and the merge driver is registered against that name, so the name has to be pinned before merge work starts.

memories.content: This is a second, independent argument for the authored acknowledgement label, which was adopted on trust-direction grounds: it is also the only form that survives the superseding memory being unavailable. Resolution otherwise goes as far as the loaded sets allow, returning the furthest memory that is loaded when the tip's set is not.
memories.why: A label justified twice from unrelated directions is one that will survive either argument being revisited, which is worth recording separately from the original case.

memories.content: The base is updated on import and on export, because both establish agreement. Updating it only on import would make the next import read every locally exported change as an incoming change from origin, and the whole file would arrive as a conflict.
memories.why: The asymmetric version is the one someone writes first, because import is where reconciliation visibly happens, and its failure appears one cycle later at the far end of the operation.

memories.content: The gate runs as part of the export-before-commit convention, at the point where a git diff of the memory files for this export-and-commit cycle is available.
memories.why: The convention was once described in a way that read as though it also produced the memories, which it does not; this document depending on the export reading is part of what prompted the description to be split.

memories.content: Two clients, the same binary, the same session, and every difference is in how each treats the parts of JSON Schema that express alternatives. Scalar types, properties, required, items, enum and description survive both. Top-level alternation is merged by one and dropped by the other; nested alternation and a nullable union type are preserved by one and reduced to nothing by the other.
memories.why: The consequence on the reduced side is not cosmetic: a property published as nothing carries no type, so an object argument is serialised as text and arrives as a string. On that client no shared set could be named at all.

memories.content: The criterion for superseding is what was believed, not what was true. The reading that kept collapsing was that supersession is for a memory that was correct when written; it gives no answer for a misunderstanding, which is exactly the case where history matters most.
memories.why: What supersession preserves is a record of what the project believed, and that value does not depend on the belief having been true.

memories.content: The golden rule document exists to be in context while conventions are drafted, and through those conventions while memories are created. It is not a preamble to be read once and set aside.
memories.why: A principle consulted once becomes a principle compiled from memory, and compiling from memory is what produced conventions that had lost the axis. Being a standing input is a property the document claims about itself because the failure mode is otherwise invisible.

memories.content: For a shared set, create is where the set name is first bound on this machine. The naming decision cannot come from the file, since a header is untrusted content, nor from the path, since a project's directory name and its set name need not coincide. It comes from whoever runs create, the only participant that knows what the set is for.
memories.why: It does not bind the name to a checkout, and this was once claimed wrongly -- create takes a name and nothing else, so no directory is in scope when it runs. The claim was doubly misleading because it presented an open question as half-answered by an operation that cannot see a checkout.

memories.content: The second check is an LLM-judgment review of whether a memory's chosen scope still looks right and whether its content reads as something that should not be in this set -- for instance, looking personal despite being scoped to a project.
memories.why: It is the check that needs meaning rather than pattern, which is why it is the LLM's and why it cannot be folded into the mechanical scan.

memories.content: An earlier draft described import as an upsert that left store-only memories alone, and located the whole distinction from restore in what happens to store-only memories. That cannot work while absence means deletion: the documented way to forget was to delete a line, so an upsert would have left the export-pull-merge-import cycle incapable of ever forgetting anything.
memories.why: The earlier version had the mechanism wrong and the conclusion right, which is worth recording because the wrong mechanism was the more attractive one. The implementation had it right and the draft was overturning working code without noticing what the code was protecting.

memories.content: A fork copies the repository header included, so the fork's memories continue to claim the original set name. Whether that is right depends on something no software can see: a contributor that will merge back should keep the name, while a divergence that will not should rename, because two histories claiming one identity will eventually be imported onto one machine and the merge will produce a set that never existed.
memories.why: The collision is what needs a human, not the naming. A set name never seen before can be bound silently because nothing existing can be contaminated; a name already bound to a different checkout is the case to refuse and surface, and a fork is the ordinary way that happens rather than an exotic one.
