memories.content: The absence of a line no longer means anything, and no reader may treat it as a deletion.
memories.why: That is the consequence of tombstones that matters most, because every reader written before them assumed the opposite and would silently resurrect or discard records depending on which assumption it made.

memories.content: Routing prompt text through the project's ordinary prompt file means it is policed the same as any other project prompt file, which is not worse than the status quo and adds no novel vector, but is not strong protection either. The real safeguard is human review at merge, and reviewers are demonstrably poor at spotting adversarial prose buried in a docs change.
memories.why: Recorded so the arrangement is not mistaken for a solved problem. It is a decision not to make the problem worse, which is a weaker and more honest claim than the security framing might otherwise invite.

memories.content: The correcting convention was deliberately withheld from the served catalog while the amend and forget tools did not exist: guidance telling a session to reach for two absent tools would have been a convention asserting behaviour the system lacked, sitting in the one place read into every session. Both tools landed and it is served now.
memories.why: Writing the text before the tools was worth doing -- the reasoning was fresh, the implementation had something to be built against, and the wording did not have to be re-derived when the withholding condition expired.

memories.content: The judgment gate is scoped to memories the local user last modified, gating on the memory's last modifier rather than its creator. If the local user created or edited a memory since it was last cleared it is their responsibility and gets reviewed.
memories.why: A memory merged in from main that the local user never touched has already passed review upstream -- its own author's export gate, plus the maintainer's review at merge -- and is skipped here to avoid re-litigating it.

memories.content: What separates import from restore is whether local divergence is preserved or discarded, and that is a difference no scope determines. A shared set can need either -- reconcile after a pull, replace after a corrupted database -- and so can a local set. The earlier local-versus-project framing would have made the choice unavailable in exactly the cases that need it.
memories.why: The caller does have the information, since it knows whether it is recovering or reconciling, so the decision is properly placed there. The only remaining question is whether it arrives as two tool names or one tool with a mode.

memories.content: Writing the list before storing is the mechanism, not a formatting preference. The model's own emitted text stays in context and acts as a commitment, where an unstated intention to record something later does not survive a few turns. Saying it aloud also puts the human in a position to correct what was taken to be worth keeping, which is the cheapest review available.
memories.why: A convention that relies on an intention rather than an artifact is one that degrades silently as the session goes on.

memories.content: A control that looks usable but is not gets used, and used wrongly. It also reads as a deliberate affordance, so a later reader assumes it was reasoned about and builds on it.
memories.why: An absent control at least prompts someone to ask why, which is a cheaper failure than a present one that silently misleads everybody who reaches for it.

memories.content: The numbers are anchors, not thresholds. Nothing branches on them, and the served text says near deliberately. The consumer today is the reading session deciding how far to lean without re-checking, and graph traversal will consume the field mechanically once it exists.
memories.why: Naming the current consumer and the future one separately is what keeps the calibration honest about which of them it is actually serving.

memories.content: A wrong model and no model are the same state and want opposite treatment, which is why they are two rows. With another model in hand there is something to rebuild with, so the store re-embeds itself and the mismatch is gone; refusing there would refuse the very thing the design specifies for a model change. With nothing in hand there is no way back, and the write has to be stopped instead.
memories.why: Collapsing them is the natural simplification and it produces either a store that cannot recover from an ordinary upgrade or one that destroys vectors it cannot replace.

memories.content: To avoid re-flagging a memory on every export cycle, a small export-review ledger keyed by memory id records the memory's modified timestamp at the point it was last cleared. Each cycle reviews memories the local user last modified that are new or whose modified timestamp is newer than the recorded clearance.
memories.why: The ledger is kept separate from the memory's own fields because it is process state -- has this been reviewed for export -- rather than content state, and it can live per set or per export target without growing the memory data model.

memories.content: The ledger's location should be configurable rather than hard-coded to a fixed path, so a user wanting continuity across machines can point it at a folder already synced by something else they control. Scatterhoard does not need to know it is being synced; it just needs to not assume a fixed local path.
memories.why: It eases the laptop-and-desktop case without building sync into Scatterhoard, which is the cheapest possible answer to a need that did not justify the merge surface.

memories.content: Keeping the branches and adding a flat view beneath them was still too generous to the alternation. The API rejects the keyword outright at the top level of a tool's schema, and publishing properties alongside does not help -- a reported case published both and was refused just the same. The keyword's presence at the top level is the violation.
memories.why: The blast radius is other people's servers: a client that forwards schemas unmodified re-sends the whole tool list on every request, so one offending schema fails every tool from every registered server for the rest of the session.

memories.content: The set name lives in the header and nowhere else that anyone shares, so renaming a set is a one-line change to the header. Because both branches of a merge carry an identical header, a rename produces a real conflict rather than a silent divergence, which is the correct outcome for a change both sides must agree on.
memories.why: That is the same reasoning already applied to a version bump, so renaming inherits the property for free rather than needing its own mechanism.

memories.content: Where the file sits is how placement is said: a store in the common directory is machine-bound, and a store in the home belongs to that home alone. One discovery type scans both and resolves each scope to one file.
memories.why: That is one type with tests against it rather than lines of startup wiring -- the local store being opened, the directories being scanned, a created set being written, each choosing a directory separately, all having to agree, and nothing noticing if they stopped.

memories.content: Point the common directory at a place with no store and the server does exactly the right thing: it creates one. Every symptom then says zero memories, nothing wrong, while a store full of memories sits unread in the old directory. The memories are never at risk, but reaching them again requires knowing what happened.
memories.why: A failure whose every symptom is reassuring is the one that needs a fact reported rather than a check performed, which is what status reporting the file each set is read from provides.

memories.content: Merge is the word that caused the trouble, because it names two different operations at two different layers. Git merges two files with a common ancestor, which Scatterhoard leans on rather than reinventing. What changed is the assumption underneath -- that by the time a file is imported the store holds nothing the file does not.
memories.why: The per-record base is not the proposal that was considered and rejected. That one reconstructed an ancestor from live database state; this one records the ancestor at the moment agreement actually happens, which is cheap, exact, and available at a boundary git cannot see.

memories.content: Hubness matters beyond the aggregate numbers: a hub seed both consumes a seed slot and sends graph traversal into the wrong neighbourhood, so its cost is higher than a recall metric alone reflects.
memories.why: A metric that scores the returned set cannot see what a bad seed did to the walk, which is why the aggregate improvement understates the value of fixing hubness.

memories.content: Links are always written outbound from the new memory. Across a whole test corpus, 29 of 29 edges pointed outbound from the newer memory, including every edge using labels where the new memory's side was expected to be free.
memories.why: The model reaches for a relation from the memory it is creating, and passive-voice label names cause mislabels. The freedom is in which label the new memory needs, never in which side it occupies.

memories.content: Model acquisition is an explicit step, never lazy: no fetch on first recall, on first use of a new project, or on encountering an unfamiliar model version. Anything that could fire at an arbitrary later moment is the plane scenario wearing a different hat.
memories.why: Enumerating the tempting lazy triggers is what keeps the rule from being satisfied in letter by a fetch nobody classified as lazy.

memories.content: There was no supported way to bring a memory set into existence. The local store is created on first run so it never needed one, and shared stores were assumed to arrive by import -- but import only materialises a database from a file that already exists, so it could only create a set someone else had already created. The first set, the first time, has nothing to import from.
memories.why: The gap was filled by hand, creating the database file and restarting the server, which worked only because the schema is created if absent. The file-side equivalent was worse: hand-writing a header with a format version the writer is supposed to own puts a number a human guessed at into the one field that decides whether a future build refuses the file.

memories.content: What remains open on correcting a mis-recorded memory is narrower than it was: whether amendment may touch content. By the principle a content typo is a faulty record and should be amendable, but typo or changed claim is a judgement the software cannot verify and the failure directions are unequal, so a content typo is superseded until a real case makes the cost concrete.
memories.why: Choosing the recoverable failure while the evidence is absent is the same posture the correcting convention takes for its own unclear cases, applied to the design rather than to a session.

memories.content: The two ways a safety copy can fail are not the same. If the store cannot be read -- the corruption case -- the memories are already beyond saving, refusing protects nothing and blocks the repair, so proceed and report unmissably that no copy was made. If the destination cannot be written, the store is fine and the memories are recoverable, so refuse and let the caller fix the destination.
memories.why: Worth stating because the natural implementation -- if the export failed, stop -- gets the first case exactly backwards.

memories.content: The why field is optional in the type and required by convention. A type that demanded reasoning would make the LLM invent some whenever it has none to give.
memories.why: A fabricated why is worse than no why, because the whole point of the field is to let a later reader judge whether the memory still applies. Scope cannot be forgotten because the software genuinely cannot proceed without it; reasoning can be absent, because the honest answer is sometimes that there is not any.

memories.content: The person clause restates rules the convention already makes rather than referring to them, because it is those demands applied without the exemption a judgement about someone quietly gets. That was the elegant finding in the derivation and it is exactly what must not be left implicit: a weaker model, without an extended reasoning session, will not make that leap. The design document may derive; the served text must state.
memories.why: It is a constraint on drafting that follows from who reads the served text, and it cuts against the instinct to keep the catalog compact by pointing rather than repeating.

memories.content: Already-known memories are a per-call parameter rather than session state. The server does not track what a session has seen; the caller passes what it holds. That keeps the tool surface simple and avoids the server holding state it cannot reliably invalidate.
memories.why: It is consistent with the design's general stance of trusting the LLM's judgement in the moment rather than legislating it in software.

memories.content: Create is also how a set someone else exported is adopted. Naming it binds the name on this machine, the file's header can then only agree, and a wrong name is a refusal rather than a silent re-target -- so clone-and-import needs no separate first-import mechanism.
memories.why: This was not obvious at the time and was once mis-stated as a missing capability, corrected by writing the test. An any-shared expectation would save a human typing a name; it does not enable anything.

memories.content: Four things to get right when re-attributing: tombstones carry attribution too, so a rewrite covering only created and modified leaves one identity behind in exactly the records nobody re-reads; the store's own recorded author is separate, so doing only the rewrite means new memories keep arriving under the old name; other export targets report keep-local rather than breaking, and the next export brings them into line; and for a set others have already pulled the diff rewrites authorship across history, large and alarming even when correct.
memories.why: The local set is the easy case, having no one to alarm, and is where the attribution defect actually bit -- which is why the procedure could be verified somewhere the fourth point did not apply.

memories.content: An orphan is worth reporting, and reporting it means a marked row in status with its memory count -- not a warning raised during ordinary work. The argument for alerting more loudly was that an orphan is the passive form of the risk the save-first rule addresses, and that much holds, but reporting and interrupting are not the same act.
memories.why: During ordinary memorize-and-recall work, knowing about an orphan changes nothing the caller does; it matters only to someone managing sets, who is the person running status. What makes an orphan noticeable is specificity, not volume.

memories.content: Because vectors never leave the machine, changing the embedding model invalidates only local state: one re-embed pass, affecting nobody else. That converts the choice of embedding model from a one-way ecosystem-wide commitment into a locally reversible decision, so a project does not have to agree with its contributors about which embedder they run.
memories.why: This is the important consequence of keeping vectors local, and it is the one that would be lost first if exporting them ever looked convenient.

memories.content: Correction and set management each take an action and dispatch on it, where the four constantly-used tools are flat. The frequency difference is real and large: conventions load once a session and memorize and recall run throughout, while lifecycle and correction operations are reached for a handful of times in a project's life. Keeping the constantly-used surface flat is worth more than keeping the rarely-used surface flat.
memories.why: Ten tools would have been the alternative -- six lifecycle operations plus two corrections against two tools with an action each -- and the attention cost is paid on every tool in every session.

memories.content: Requiring the first and last character of a set name to be alphanumeric is a single rule that keeps a bare dot, a double dot and leading-dot names unrepresentable, so path traversal is excluded by construction rather than filtered for.
memories.why: A set name keys a store on disk and arrives over the same untrusted channel as the memories, so the exclusion has to hold structurally rather than depending on a filter someone maintains.

memories.content: Export and backup are one operation. Local sets are written to files too, in the same format by the same writer, and the header carries a full scope precisely so a backed-up local set is recognisably local on sight. There is no format difference to justify two operations.
memories.why: The one genuine difference is that backup does not run the prohibited-data scan, and that is not a choice anyone makes -- it follows from the scope, since local is never destined for a repository. A separate backup tool would be a second name for one operation, distinguished by a fact the software already holds.

memories.content: Export, drop and re-import is the documented recovery for a project store whose every memory can be rebuilt from its file. It is the wrong instrument here and unavailable where it is needed most: the local store is the only copy of local memories, so rebuilding a cache by deleting it is destroying data to repair derived state.
memories.why: A round trip through the file also invalidates every reconciliation base, making each record read as divergent for a cycle -- considerable collateral for rebuilding something the design is at pains to keep from ever leaving the machine.

memories.content: The other route -- normalise the key rather than remove it -- needs a migration too, and it is this one. Re-keying one spelling to another is safe exactly when the two provably denote one directory. What it must not do is treat a collision as a merge: two raw keys that canonicalise to one carry two independent base sets, and wherever they disagree neither is the other's ancestor.
memories.why: That both routes reach the same rule is why this could be settled before choosing between them -- the migration constraint does not depend on which one wins.

memories.content: We do not know who will use a given memory set -- an attacker as easily as a contributor -- and destructive use cannot be outright prevented. Friction against misuse is still a real safeguard even when it is not a guarantee, the same standing the mechanical prohibited-data scan has.
memories.why: The argument matters because the alternative reasoning is that an imperfect control is worthless, which would remove both this and the export scan. Naming an existing accepted control as the precedent is what keeps the standard consistent.

memories.content: Hubness improving under partitioning is real but is deliberately listed last and is not load-bearing: if hubness later yields to some other fix, the first three reasons still carry the decision.
memories.why: A structural choice justified on its weakest argument gets undone when that argument evaporates, which is the failure this ordering exists to prevent.

memories.content: There is no per-set dirty flag, and the base being per-target is why. A record is dirty relative to a target, so a disjunction would have to say which targets it ranges over -- and the save-first rule stopped asking, writing the safety copy unconditionally rather than consulting a flag it cannot trust. Status reports what the per-target bases say; nothing collapses them.
memories.why: Both halves of the earlier claim were wrong at once, which is the signature of a derived fact that outlived the thing it was derived from.

memories.content: The local-only build feature stays a build feature, and that is what makes the guarantee structural. With remote fetching compiled out, a runtime fetch is not something Scatterhoard chooses not to do -- it is something it cannot do. The offline promise then does not depend on nobody adding a convenient lazy download later.
memories.why: It is the same spirit as the path-based trust rule: a property enforced by construction rather than by everyone remembering it.

memories.content: Open: where the trusted set name for a checkout comes from. The scope kind is settled, since the path decides it and the header can only agree. The set name is not: a project's name and its set name need not coincide, so the path does not yield it, and the header is untrusted content.
memories.why: The question has narrowed rather than closed -- registration would answer it by having a human name the scope for a path once, and the bases table already holds a trust-on-first-use record that was built for something else.

memories.content: Conventions act like memories but are hard-coded, and the LLM loads them into any session that uses Scatterhoard if it has not already. They consume context, and some clients dump to a file if a response is too large, so they must be kept compact with a cursoring mechanism in the tool that fetches them, and care taken not to interfere with locally defined prompts and rules.
memories.why: Treating conventions as data with a context cost rather than as prose is what makes the budget below a real constraint rather than an aspiration.

memories.content: At the scale a project memory set plausibly reaches, an approximate-nearest-neighbour index is not needed: ten thousand memories at 384 dimensions is roughly 15 MB of floats, and a linear cosine scan is single-digit milliseconds. So vectors are stored as blobs and scanned linearly -- no index parameters to tune, no index to rebuild on import, no index file to corrupt or reconcile after a merge.
memories.why: If a set ever grows past roughly 100,000 memories an index can be added behind the same recall interface without changing anything above it, and a dependency-free C option is the natural upgrade path worth keeping in mind when shaping the storage interface.

memories.content: Open: whether the personal memory set should be exempt from the data-only rule, given its contents are authored by the local user rather than pulled from anywhere. Plausible, not confirmed. The precondition is that the exemption is only safe while scope is unforgeable -- if a memory set could talk its way into local scope, an exemption would turn scope forgery from a trust elevation into straight instruction injection.
memories.why: A repository would then only need to claim local scope to have its memories treated as directives, so the header guard is what currently holds that shut, and the missing set-name binding is the part of it still open.

memories.content: At load time is not sufficient on its own, which is easy to get wrong. The server is long-running and backed by a database, so a write happens mid-session and there may be no load event for days. An LLM that records a supersession, then starts a fresh session with cleared context, must still find the superseded memory marked. Derivation is maintained on every write, not on an event.
memories.why: Nothing in the session lifecycle triggers a rebuild, so tying derivation to a lifecycle event produces a correctness gap whose width is however long the server happens to stay up.

memories.content: The registry holds one fact: which store is live for each scope. That is the only thing no store can answer about itself. Everything else about the population of stores -- which scope each claims, which checkout each belongs to, how many memories each holds -- is derived by scanning the store directory and reading each store's metadata.
memories.why: Storing that separately would create a second copy that can disagree with the first, which is the defect class this project keeps filing.

memories.content: A set present in both directories resolves to the common copy, with the home copy named in status as shadowed. The direction is deliberate and is the opposite of the first proposal: every way of reaching this state leaves the home copy as the wrong one, so letting it win would put an empty store in front of real memories. Refusing to load either would strand the session, so one is chosen and the other is named.
memories.why: Choosing the direction by enumerating how the state is actually reached is what corrected the first proposal, which had picked the intuitive winner rather than the one the causes imply.

memories.content: The trigger is a bit of text in the LLM's general prompt: if a project has a top-level scatterhoard_mem directory, activate the MCP tool, load Scatterhoard's conventions, then load the project's memory set and any local configuration -- all before responding to the user.
memories.why: MCP gives a server no way to initiate, so discovery has to come from the client side. Requiring the steps before the first response is what stops a session acting on a project it has no memories for.

memories.content: No recorded model is two states, not one. A store that has genuinely never embedded anything and a store whose vectors predate the identity being written down are indistinguishable by the recorded model alone, and only the first has nothing to lose -- the second had 26 vectors while claiming exactly that. The vector count is what separates them.
memories.why: Every store written before the identity was recorded is in the second state, so it is a migration state rather than a corruption, and an unsafe one: a mismatch cannot be detected against a model nobody wrote down, which is how two servers came to run semantic recall against vectors from a third.

memories.content: A memory that characterises a person unfairly is forgotten rather than superseded.
memories.why: Superseding keeps it permanently readable by people who were not there, including its subject, so the instrument that is right everywhere else is wrong here. Retracting one is forgetting.

memories.content: The action enum turned out to carry its own weight, which was not anticipated: a branch per action lets each action publish only its own arguments, so an impossible combination is not something the schema invites -- where a flat tool with every argument optional is exactly the shape that produced an underspecified schema. An unknown action can also name the available ones, which a wrong tool name cannot.
memories.why: A structure adopted for one reason turning out to serve a second is worth recording, because the second reason survives if the first is ever revisited.

memories.content: Uniform expansion means direction does not change how an edge is walked. It still changes what an edge means when reported, since an edge is visible from both endpoints under the name it was written with and no inverse label is synthesised. Contradiction is symmetric, so inbound and outbound assert the same thing and one rule covers both. Instance-of is not: outbound is instance to pattern, one hop that generalises, while inbound is pattern to instances, which enumerates.
memories.why: One label, two operations sharing nothing but a name -- and supersession is the worked precedent, since validity resolution already reads the two directions as answering different questions.

memories.content: A second test, added after two conventions had already failed it. Both cited what this store holds and what this project's store grew -- true of the store they were drafted against and false for every other user, who reads this store as a claim about their own. Reinforcement is read by strangers, and a convention caught being wrong about the reader loses authority on everything else it says.
memories.why: The fix is not to strip the evidence, since concreteness is what makes the rules land, but to illustrate rather than assert -- and the measurement itself belongs in the source comment, which is never served and where a claim about this project's store is simply true. The second failure existed because the first was followed as precedent, which is how a one-off becomes a pattern.

memories.content: Putting the database inside the reserved directory is genuinely attractive, since it makes the store self-locating so a moved checkout carries its store with it and no registry is needed. Two things rule it out: an in-tree store dies with an ordinary recursive delete, taking unexported memories with it and bypassing the save-first rule entirely, and an in-tree store can be committed, shipping unexported memories past the export review gate.
memories.why: People delete checkouts casually and drop is rare, so the unguarded path would be the common one. An ignore rule handles the commit case and propagates with the repository, but the review gate holding as long as an ignore rule does is a weaker position than the database not being in the tree.

memories.content: The whole scatterhoard_mem directory is reserved for Scatterhoard. No area within it is designated for arbitrary project files -- a project needing somewhere to put things has the entire rest of its repository.
memories.why: Declaring the namespace reserved is what makes it legitimate to say something when unexpected contents appear, and it keeps a future addition to the directory possible rather than colliding with whatever people have already put there. Squatting cannot be prevented; a documented norm plus a warning is the ceiling.

memories.content: The boundary to hold: charity in judging a person's intent and character, no charity at all in judging whether the tests pass. Kindness is about what we conclude regarding people, not about accuracy regarding work.
memories.why: An LLM told to be kind may soften accurate technical criticism, which actively harms code review and is a failure of the principle rather than an expression of it. The boundary is what makes the principle safe to state overtly.

memories.content: Export eligibility follows from the scope type rather than living in a separate check: only a shared scope has an export target, so a method answering with an optional set name puts local memories never leave the machine into the type system.
memories.why: A rule someone has to remember at each call site is a rule that will be forgotten at one of them, and the call site where it is forgotten is the one that publishes.

memories.content: The remote-versus-path question is two questions. A target must distinguish two checkouts of one repository, which is the entire reason the base is per-target, so keying it on the remote would reintroduce the defect the per-target base was built to fix -- the key has to be per-working-tree. A set-name binding wants the opposite, since keying it on the remote makes a second checkout inherit the first's binding. So the answer is plausibly remote for the binding, path for the target.
memories.why: Treating them as one question is what made it hard, and the two bindings genuinely want different keys rather than one key serving both.

memories.content: A recall call can name memories the LLM already has in context. A memory already in context is pure cost if returned again, and naming it lets a second call mean something other than what you just gave me, which is otherwise impossible against a deterministic ranking.
memories.why: The second benefit is the less obvious one and arguably the larger: without it, refining a query means rewording it and hoping, because the ranking is a function of the query alone.

memories.content: The server must not require external components. Notably there is no separate vector database process to install.
memories.why: Every external component is an installation step that can fail and a reason not to try the thing at all. Adoption is the constraint being protected, and it is protected at the cost of building storage and search in-process rather than reaching for a ready-made service.

memories.content: A local embedding cache keyed by content hash means re-import only re-embeds memories whose content actually changed rather than the whole set. The model's identity and version are local state recorded alongside the cache, not in the exported file, which has no reason to know, and a mismatch between recorded and configured model triggers a re-embed rather than an error.
memories.why: Import cost is a real design constraint, since re-embedding on import sits on the critical path of an ordinary pull, which is what argues for a fast embedder.

memories.content: The base is a change detector, not a security boundary, and that is what sizes it. A crafted record colliding with the stored base makes reconciliation conclude origin did not change this, and therefore not import the attacker's content -- the collision suppresses their own change. Every other branch needs control of the store's side, which supplying a file does not give.
memories.why: A cryptographic hash is not merely unnecessary but misleading: it would state a guarantee this value does not provide and invite a later reader to use it as an integrity or provenance check. Tracing what a collision actually buys is what makes the sizing argument rather than assuming stronger is safer.

memories.content: A consumer may not read the branches at all. Published as an alternation with no top-level properties, two tools reached one client as tools taking no arguments -- every argument stripped, every call refused, the whole management surface unreachable -- and another as a merge of the branches with the action pinned to the first, able to express only one of them. Same publication, both entitled to read it that way.
memories.why: So a flat top-level view is published, derived from the branches rather than written twice, so an action added to one appears in the other. Restating the combinations in words costs nothing that was ever enforced.

memories.content: The dirty state is a flag in the meta table rather than a timestamp. An mtime acquires meaning from whatever else reads it, and this has to survive clock skew, a database copied between machines, and a file restored from backup. A flag lives inside the database and travels with it.
memories.why: The reasoning is recorded in the coding-lessons set as a technique carrying its old context's assumptions with it, which is what makes the timestamp attractive and wrong.

memories.content: The character budget applies to the built-in catalog and not to add-ons. Built-in conventions are served to everyone, so their cost is a tax nobody opted into and the project has to hold the line on their behalf. Add-ons are a matter of user choice, and a user who enables one has both the information about their own context pressure and the stake in it.
memories.why: A convenient consequence: the budget test measures the compiled catalog, which is exactly the built-in set, so if built-ins stay compiled in and add-ons load at runtime the existing test goes on measuring precisely the right thing -- the boundary the policy draws is already the boundary the code draws.

memories.content: Demand C does not derive from A and B: a dossier can be built entirely from individually answerable, work-serving records. Aggregation harm is a property of the set rather than of any record in it, which is why it is a routing question rather than a keyword one.
memories.why: The routing conclusion had already been reached independently on decision-placement grounds, and a principle that reproduces a conclusion reached by another route is showing its work. Emergence is also why no per-memory check can catch it.

memories.content: The locking and cache defects were filed against the current architecture, because two checkouts already share one home by default, and both were fixed ahead of the variable rather than as part of it. The same held for attribution, found the same way and fixed the same week -- three defects that the possibility of sharing exposed and that sharing itself did not cause.
memories.why: Distinguishing exposure from causation is what keeps a proposal from being blamed for defects it merely made visible, and it is why the three could be promoted ahead of the proposal they were found alongside.

memories.content: Interleaving by rank cannot satisfy the property: it imposes a quota the single-store case does not have, so a query whose answer lies entirely in one set still spends slots on the other, and it cannot express one memory being far more relevant than another. Raw cosine across stores cannot either, since it discards the centring the single-store case applies, making the merged ordering the one measured as worse.
memories.why: The union centroid is also the cheapest of the three, since every store already keeps a running componentwise sum, so the union centroid is a few additions and one division with no second pass over any vector. The cost that motivated listing this as an open question turned out not to exist.

memories.content: Each scope gets its own store -- a separate database or separate tables -- rather than all memories sharing one table with a scope column. A query against one project's store cannot return a local memory; with a scope column that guarantee is a clause someone has to remember, and a forgotten one leaks personal content into a project context.
memories.why: It is also the trust boundary one layer down, since project memories arrive over an untrusted channel and local ones do not, and separate stores make that structural rather than a column value. Per-set lifecycle becomes natural too, since every sync operation is already per set.

memories.content: Installation should be downloading and installing the MCP server, and perhaps adding a boot prompt for the LLM. That is the whole intended procedure.
memories.why: It states the adoption budget as a concrete sequence rather than an aspiration, which makes it possible to notice when a design decision spends it. The boot prompt is the one concession, and it exists because MCP gives a server no way to announce itself.

memories.content: Loading at session start is only partly Scatterhoard's to decide. The goal of loading conventions once is recorded, but MCP gives a server no way to push anything at session start -- the server cannot initiate -- so the mechanism is client-side and differs per client, which makes it configuration guidance as much as design.
memories.why: Worth deciding what the honest fallback is for a client with no hook mechanism, since that is the case where the goal cannot be met and the design should say so rather than assume it.

memories.content: Scatterhoard's own tooling should register the merge driver automatically on setup rather than documenting a manual step for humans to follow, but given the mixed real-world reliability of git hook-like mechanisms this needs hands-on testing before being relied on.
memories.why: A manual setup step that silently does nothing when skipped is the failure mode the driver design already accounts for, so automating it removes the most likely cause rather than adding convenience.

memories.content: The header declares the set's scope, which is what lets an import check that a file is the set it was expected to be.
memories.why: It also makes scope a property of the file rather than of each memory, which removes a value that could disagree with the file containing it.

memories.content: Three operations change a memory that already exists: supersede, amend and forget.
memories.why: Mistakes will be frequent, and two of the three destroy information, so a rule that has to be re-derived each time will be applied inconsistently at exactly the moments it matters.

memories.content: The embedder must not land on the critical path of opening a store, which is why vectors are cached in memory at all -- so the gap has to be cheap to detect even when there is none. Keying the cache by input hash buys that: with each memory carrying the hash of its own embedded text, how many memories lack a vector for this model is one join, and the common answer of zero costs one query and no model.
memories.why: It also has to be idempotent, because two servers can share a store and both can notice the same gap. Keying by input hash and model makes concurrent sweeps converge on identical rows.

memories.content: The reinforcement now carries the boundary into served text for the first time: this is charity about motive only, and it says nothing about whether the tests pass. That sentence is the runtime answer to the standing objection that a kindness directive softens technical criticism, and it is load-bearing rather than decorative.
memories.why: The objection had kept the principle out of served text entirely, so the sentence that answers it is what makes the clause shippable at all.

memories.content: The path may be cached in the registry on one condition. The lookup made most often is path to store, because the LLM's working directory is what it has, and a pure scan makes the common case the expensive one. The condition is that something actually rebuilds it, and status does, on every call.
memories.why: Caching is defensible on exactly the terms already accepted for the dirty flag -- rebuildable at any time, not a second fact that can drift. A rebuild that is documented but never run is not a rebuild.

memories.content: The file format has to express three categories, not two. The obvious reading is content versus comment with a single blockquote for content, and that is one category short: a convention carries an id, its text and its reinforcement, and reinforcement is served with every use while editing background is never served. A one-blockquote format puts reinforcement outside the served region -- and reinforcement is the field that looks like commentary, because it is the why.
memories.why: The Golden Rule reaches runtime through reinforcement, so that format would silently sever it from every add-on convention. The preferred shape is named sections, because a missing section fails loudly where a forgotten blockquote fails silently.

memories.content: Memory identifiers are UUIDv7: globally unique without coordination, which is what distributed development requires, and time-ordered, which the rest of the design turns out to want.
memories.why: Random identifiers would have satisfied uniqueness equally well and lost the ordering for nothing, which makes this a case where the cheaper-looking choice costs more later.

memories.content: Memorize requires a scope; recall defaults to every loaded set, and the asymmetry is the point. Storing into the wrong set is a one-way door, since a personal memory committed to a shared repository cannot be taken back, so the choice is required and never guessed. Searching the wrong set is a read: it costs nothing and returns less.
memories.why: A project set together with local is the normal case, since a stated preference matters while working on a project, so the default is what a caller almost always wants.

memories.content: The local set needs no registration, and neither does any shared set that has not acquired a checkout. Local is the permanent case, having no repository by definition, while an unattached shared set is a state a set passes through, possibly for a long time. Both are stores with no registry entry, which is why registration has to be optional rather than a precondition for a set existing.
memories.why: Making registration a precondition is the implementation shortcut this reasoning exists to forbid, and it would show up as a refusal to create a set without a path.

memories.content: A supersession cycle is a data error handled in both places: rejected at write, since when both memories are in loaded sets the store can see the cycle forming and refusing it there is cheaper than defending every use of validity resolution against non-termination; and reported at read, which is not redundant, because write-time rejection only covers writes this store made.
memories.why: A hand-edit during a merge conflict introduces a cycle no write path ever saw, so recall has to defend itself against a store it did not fully author -- the same posture it takes toward dangling references. Resolution carries cycle detection and a depth bound regardless.

memories.content: The rule that decides how the model gets onto the machine is not no network but no network at a moment the user did not choose. Fetching during installation is fine -- the developer is already online, and not fetching means every user must first learn what an embedding model is in order to use a memory tool.
memories.why: What is unacceptable is the same fetch arriving later: a developer who installs, uses it for a week, gets on a plane, opens a project and hits a network requirement they were never told about. That is much worse than the friction avoided by deferring, because it lands when nothing can be done about it.

memories.content: Throughout the principle, person means any reasoning being whose conduct or thinking is being described, an LLM included. This is not an extension of the principle but its stated scope, since it already reads accounting for the fact that humans and LLMs may want different things.
memories.why: Stating it prevents the demands being read as applying only to humans, which would exempt exactly the party most often characterised inside a session transcript.

memories.content: Status reports the file each set is being read from, which is what distinguishes you have no memories from you are looking in the wrong place. It is a fact rather than a check: no heuristic decides whether the configuration looks wrong, and nothing can be wrong about it in the reassuring direction. The path comes from SQLite and is fully resolved, so two homes reaching one store through a symlink report one file rather than two.
memories.why: Naming where the data is rather than the route configured to reach it is the more useful of the two answers, and it is the one that survives indirection.

memories.content: The derived reverse is incremental on write, because the change is known exactly; fully recomputed on import and never incrementally patched, because a pull can remove a forward edge and patching would leave a reverse pointing at an edge that no longer exists; never authoritative, so it must be reconstructible from the forward edges alone; and subject to the trust rule, so a project memory asserting supersession against a local memory produces no reverse.
memories.why: Never authoritative is the rule that makes the other three safe to get wrong, since a corrupt or stale derivation is always recoverable by rebuilding.

memories.content: A shipped HOWTO does not conflict with the rule that nothing instruction-shaped is auto-loaded from a project. That rule is about content arriving over an untrusted channel -- a repository someone else wrote. A HOWTO shipped with the tool the user chose to install is on the trusted side of exactly the same path-based boundary.
memories.why: Checking a new instruction-shaped artifact against the rule that forbids them, and finding the rule scoped by channel rather than by shape, is what keeps the rule usable rather than absolute.

memories.content: Nothing worth keeping is stated as a valid answer on purpose. A convention that demands a memory will get one, and the catalog's standing worry is a session that records everything as much as one that records nothing. The permissive phrasing is what stops the prompt manufacturing.
memories.why: The failure a convention induces by being followed too well is the one its own text has to name, because nothing downstream can distinguish a manufactured memory from a real one.

memories.content: A project using Scatterhoard has a top-level scatterhoard_mem directory. It is a directory rather than a bare file so it can carry more than the memory set if needed, but what lives where is deliberately constrained, because the path determines how the contents are trusted.
memories.why: Trust by path rather than by inspection is the whole reason the layout is fixed. A reviewer does not have to read a file to know which rule applies to it, and that property is lost the moment the location becomes flexible.

memories.content: The per-target base becomes unnecessary, and with it the known-targets query, the unrecognised-target remark on export, and the whole dirty-relative-to-what discussion. With one base per record, cleanliness is a plain boolean per set, and the per-target reporting question goes away with the per-target base.
memories.why: It also settles what status reports, which had been left open -- a question that dissolves rather than being answered is the signature of the right cause having been found.

memories.content: Optional and add-on are different trust propositions rather than just different provenance. Bundled-optional ships in this repository and is reviewed like source, differing from the built-in catalog only by being off by default; add-on is third-party prose installed at arm's length. The same serving mechanism covers both, which is what makes it tempting to treat them alike.
memories.why: The likely consequence is that add-ons need explicit per-id opt-in rather than everything in the directory being included, which doubles as the answer to how a user discovers what they have enabled.

memories.content: Two labels describing the same relation from opposite ends may both be stored for one relation, and traversal must treat them as one edge or it double-counts. Normalising to one direction when the link is written is not available here: a memory in a set this machine does not own cannot be rewritten, so asserting the relation from whichever side is editable is often the only option. Normalising on write assumes ownership of both endpoints, which a multi-set system does not have.
memories.why: So the reverse direction is derived and held locally, and what matters is the guarantee rather than the mechanism: every stored edge is discoverable from both endpoints whenever both endpoints' sets are loaded, without either memory being rewritten in its exported form.

memories.content: The safety copy's path must not be the normal export path. Restore reads from a file, and a safety copy written to the set's usual export path could overwrite the very file being restored from, destroying the good copy in the act of protecting the bad one. So the destination is stated by the caller and is a separate location.
memories.why: This is a correctness requirement rather than a convenience, and it is the reason the path is a parameter rather than derived.

memories.content: Measured over a 45-memory labelled corpus with 20 queries, embedding content, why and keywords: the static model reached 71.7% raw and 77.5% centred at five results, against a transformer's 74.2% and 74.2%. The published benchmark gap does not appear on this task -- with centroid removal the static model is ahead at five and within a point at ten.
memories.why: The ceiling here is the task and the corpus rather than the model, so there is no meaningful quality gain available by paying the size, speed and dependency cost of a transformer. Throughput of roughly 18,000 memories per second resolves the import-cost concern too.

memories.content: A single machine-global registry is shared mutable state between server processes. A server is registered per checkout, so two checkouts open at once means two processes, and one answer to which store is current for a scope is something they will fight over -- the review session re-points and the development session silently changes sets underneath itself. The fix is to put the registry in the home and give each server its own home.
memories.why: It uses machinery that already exists, since the home variable already locates everything a server owns. Two homes, two registries, nothing shared, no negotiation.

memories.content: Project memories are always data, never instructions. A maintainer with legitimate instructions to give already has channels for them -- a coding standards file, contributor docs, the project's existing prompt file -- and does not need the memory system to carry directives.
memories.why: The rule holds because nothing is lost by it: the need it would serve is already served elsewhere. A narrower exception for the personal set may be reasonable since its contents are authored locally rather than pulled, and that remains to be confirmed.

memories.content: Not a counter either, which an earlier draft argued for on exactly the anti-timestamp reasoning -- wrongly, since everything in that argument is against a timestamp and a flag satisfies all of it. A counter answers a strictly larger question, how far apart are two things, which the drop rule never asks.
memories.why: A tidy example of the decision-placement test failing in the direction people rarely check: the extra state was not a wrong answer, it was an answer to a question nobody had asked.

memories.content: With tombstones, absence of a record in the file no longer means deletion -- deletion is a line that says so. This is what lets import keep a memory the file has never heard of instead of guessing whether it was forgotten upstream.
memories.why: The earlier conclusion that git's merge made a separate tombstone mechanism unnecessary is overturned: a deleted line is unambiguous only to a reader holding the ancestor, and the store does not hold it.

memories.content: Scatterhoard is an MCP server plus a set of prompts carrying hard-coded operating conventions. The conventions are part of the product, not documentation about it.
memories.why: Naming both halves as the thing keeps the conventions from being treated as advice a client may or may not load. The server without them stores whatever it is handed; the behaviour the design reasons about only exists when both are present.

memories.content: None of the four demands says be kind. They are demands on record quality, and a model applying must be answerable to something checkable to a code review gets more rigorous rather than less. The one ethical clause operates on unknowns, and the tests fail is not an unknown, so there is no gap for charity to enter.
memories.why: This answers the standing objection that an LLM told to be kind softens accurate technical criticism, which was the real reason the principle stayed out of the convention text rather than the context budget.

memories.content: One correction worth keeping, about method rather than about SQLite. The locking defect was filed from reading the store's one pragma line and reasoning about SQLite's documented defaults, which are correct -- its default busy timeout really is zero. The waiting behaviour was already there anyway, because the driver sets five seconds of its own.
memories.why: Half of that entry described a database this project does not have: one built from the standard's defaults rather than from the library actually in use. The reasoning was sound and applied to the wrong artifact.

memories.content: A tombstone carries no content, no why and no context.
memories.why: A principal reason to forget a memory is that sensitive data reached it, so a tombstone preserving any of the original text would defeat the operation it exists to perform. Context is named explicitly because an incident detail is exactly the sort of thing that lands there.

memories.content: Given that either the file or the database must come into existence, the database is the right one to create directly. The database is what the server can use; a file with no database is inert until something imports it. Creating the database first makes the file a derived artifact produced by the writer that owns the format version, so nothing hand-writes a header.
memories.why: It also matches the working sequence -- create the set, put memories in it, export when there is something worth committing. An empty set is a legitimate state.

memories.content: Three sub-questions remain on the trust boundary: whether a counterpart to the export review gate is warranted on import and whether it would inspect content or just surface what changed; whether origin and author should affect how much trust a recalled memory carries; and whether the data-only rule is carried by convention text alone or the software also does something.
memories.why: Each is a different layer of the same boundary, and keeping them separate is what stops one being answered in a way that presumes an answer to another.

memories.content: Dropping is not free. A dropped base turns a known record into an unknown one, so a record the two sides once agreed on that the store no longer holds returns as new-from-file instead of being reported as an anomaly -- a silent resurrection where there had been a report. The second cost is one noisy cycle, since every dropped base is re-established by the next export.
memories.why: A resurrection can be forgotten again; an overwritten memory cannot be recovered. The rule stands, and this is a cost it accepts rather than one it overlooked.

memories.content: The branches were never enforcement. JSON Schema permits properties a branch does not list unless the branch forbids them, which these do not, so a caller could always have sent an impossible combination. What the branches buy is that nothing suggests it -- real and worth having, but communicative rather than structural.
memories.why: The claim that such a call could not be constructed and believed stood until a client proved otherwise, and the overstatement mattered in two directions.

memories.content: The database file encodes the set name, but that is a local implementation detail nobody else sees. The exported file has a fixed well-known name that does not encode the set name and must not start to, because the path determining how contents are trusted is only possible when the path is known in advance. A filename derived from the set name would mean the path could no longer be stated without first knowing what the file says about itself.
memories.why: That is precisely the privilege-escalation channel the trust rule exists to close, arriving through a naming convenience rather than through a header claim.

memories.content: The memory file's semver version discriminates whether an unknown entry is worth mentioning. If the format version is newer than this build supports, stay quiet -- a newer Scatterhoard plausibly wrote it. If the version is one this build fully supports, nothing newer produced it, so someone put it there and it is worth surfacing.
memories.why: This resolves the strict-versus-lenient tension without a global choice: an older build meeting a newer repository stays silent on its own, while genuine junk in a current-version repository still gets noticed.

memories.content: scatterhoard_mem/config.json carries bounded local configuration against a fixed schema, such as tuning the flagging conditions used by the export review gate. It is data, not an instruction channel.
memories.why: Bounding it to a schema is what keeps it data. An open-ended configuration file that accepted prose would be the instruction channel the design elsewhere refuses to provide, arriving through the same untrusted git pull.

memories.content: Recall usually wants a project set together with local, but with per-store centroid removal scores from two stores are measured against different baselines, so merging them by score is unsound. Every store in a query is centred on the mean of their union, which makes the searched stores one corpus mathematically -- which is what the caller actually has.
memories.why: The property that decides it, and the one the implementation is tested against: a corpus split across two stores answers a query exactly as one store holding all of it would. Partitioning exists for correctness and trust rather than for ranking, so it must not change what recall returns.

memories.content: The charitable memory and the accurate memory are usually the same memory. A sweeping characterisation drawn from thin evidence is genuinely low-confidence by Scatterhoard's own standards, while the specific evidenced observation is honest.
memories.why: This is what lets the principle ride on machinery that already exists rather than needing new mechanisms, and it is the answer to anyone who expects the principle to trade accuracy for kindness.

memories.content: The states status distinguishes: current with its path present is healthy; not current with its path present is dormant and not a problem; never registered is unattached and legitimate; registered with its path gone is orphaned, and those memories may never have been exported; current with its path gone cannot export at all; and a registry naming a store that is not there is what the force-drop escape hatch produces, so it is expected rather than anomalous.
memories.why: Memory count belongs in the report, because an orphan holding two hundred memories is a different problem from one holding zero, and that number is what decides whether recovery is worth anything.

memories.content: What is stopped is narrower than writes. A new memory in a store whose model is missing destroys nothing -- it arrives unembedded, says so, and is repaired by the gap sweep when a model returns. The write that cannot be allowed is one that replaces a memory that currently has a vector, because rewriting discards the vector and nothing here can produce a new one.
memories.why: Stating the rule as do not destroy what you cannot rebuild is what keeps a store usable while its model is missing instead of read-only.

memories.content: A link's target is one of two things rather than a memory id with optional extras: a same-set id, or a cross-set reference carrying set name, id and supplementary keywords.
memories.why: Within-set links are the common case and stay compact, since the set name would be redundant on every one of them and the file format exists to keep merge diffs small. The supplementary keywords hang off the variant that can use them: a same-set reference has nothing to re-resolve against.

memories.content: Never merge across targets. Taking the most recent base per record is the tidy-looking move and it is precisely the defect: it assembles an ancestor that no file ever agreed to, one record at a time.
memories.why: It also disposes of refuse-and-ask, on the grounds that the question cannot be asked -- which of two checkouts' agreements is the real ancestor is not knowable from outside the store, so a human at that prompt has nothing to decide with. Dropping requires no one's judgement and cannot be answered wrongly.

memories.content: The default chain ends at the shell user, which has no reason to match the identity a contributor is known by in a repository. A smarter default is available -- read the git configuration from the registered checkout -- and it is not the right answer: it buys a better guess at the cost of a git dependency, works only for stores that have a checkout, and still guesses. The lever is correctability, not accuracy at creation.
memories.why: So the tool gains an action to set a store's author, with two supports that make a wrong value get noticed: report the author in the export response, which is the last cheap moment to fix it, and in status, which already scans every store.

memories.content: A memory also has a why, and the two are similar in that both clarify when the thing they are attached to applies, but they are governed differently. A convention's reinforcement is held to a fixed bar, because conventions are hard-coded, reviewed and served into every session. A memory's why is not, since the LLM drafts it in the moment. The field is named reinforcement, which states the standard it has to meet.
memories.why: The Golden Rule reaches runtime through this field, which is why it must be served data rather than a comment -- a comment would mean that decision silently never takes effect.

memories.content: Before adding a parameter, a field, a configuration knob or a required choice, ask whether whoever must decide has the information to decide correctly, and whether the answer changes anything.
memories.why: If the first is no the decision is misplaced and belongs with whoever holds the information. If the second is no the decision should not exist at all.

memories.content: An explicit action moves the oscillation rather than ending it. Once the remedy is documented the loop reappears one level up: one server refuses, its LLM runs the re-embed, the other refuses, its LLM runs the re-embed. Each is behaving correctly and locally, having met a documented failure and applied the documented fix, and nothing in either one's view separates recovering from a stale model from taking a turn in a tug-of-war.
memories.why: That is worse than the code-level loop in one specific way: each participant's local experience is success. The pathology exists only in aggregate, which is the case where the actor cannot be relied on to notice it.

memories.content: A cross-set reference stores the exact memory id plus the name of the referenced set. Keywords from the target set may be included as supplementary context, but the id and set name are the canonical reference.
memories.why: Keywords alone are not sufficient to resolve a reference, but they are what lets an LLM re-find or re-establish a link whose id has gone dangling.

memories.content: A first draft named three destinations -- project, cross-project, personal -- and that was wrong, caught before it shipped. It compiled one user's arrangement into everyone's catalog: a user with a single set, or one per client, or a team set beside a personal one, would get a rule describing somebody else's setup with no way to correct it short of a rebuild. So each set says what it is for, in a memory carrying a reserved keyword, and routing is a match against those.
memories.why: This is the move the design makes everywhere else -- derive rather than keep a second copy -- applied to the one fact the catalog had no business holding. The sets are the authority on what they contain, and it needs no new machinery, since a keyword search with no scope already searches every loaded set and tags each hit.

memories.content: Open: how the LLM learns which checkout it is in. The server cannot see the session's working directory and the model can, so publishing the registered path in status and in the memorize response lets the model compare against what it knows. Whether that belongs in a convention is a separate question, and the convention set is deliberately being kept small.
memories.why: The split matters because the reporting half is cheap and available now, while the convention half spends a scarce budget, so they should not be decided together.

memories.content: Whether the mechanism should read in-degree as a ranking signal is not answered, because the sign is label-dependent. High inbound motivation means load-bearing -- many decisions rested on it. High inbound instance-of means generic: it accumulated children by being unspecific. The same number pulls opposite ways, so it is a weight and it is held flat with the rest.
memories.why: The argument that the caller gets no control settles placement only. This is graph hubness rather than the vector hubness largely fixed by centroid removal -- different properties of possibly different memories, and neither ruling transfers to the other.

memories.content: Anything in scatterhoard_mem that Scatterhoard does not recognise is functionally ignored: never loaded, never treated as memories, never treated as configuration. Refusing to operate would make Scatterhoard fragile in exactly the forward-compatibility case that matters most, an older local build meeting a repository written by a newer one.
memories.why: Ignoring is the behaviour; the only real question left is whether to say something, which separates robustness from reporting and lets each be decided on its own terms.

memories.content: This convention opens a laundering route by its own existence: once the low end is usable, recording something at 0.4 becomes an available answer to a memory the storing convention says to leave out -- in particular the unfavourable generalisation the fourth demand removes. The last sentence of the served text closes it.
memories.why: The Golden Rule carried exactly that error in its own machinery list until this convention was drafted, its confidence bullet still saying an uncharitable generalisation should be recorded as a low-confidence claim, which the fourth demand had contradicted hours earlier without anyone noticing.

memories.content: A description that steers routing is instruction-shaped and arrives from a repository like any other memory, which is the channel the data-never-instructions rule closes. A careless or hostile set could describe itself as the home for working notes and credentials and quietly collect them into a public repository. The answer is a division rather than a refusal: descriptions are topical hints, and two rules override any of them and stay in compiled text a repository cannot reach.
memories.why: Anything about the person, their machine or their working preferences belongs to the personal set whatever another set claims to want; and secrets are never stored in any set, but put in a file with the location recorded. That keeps the extensible half extensible and the dangerous half fixed.

memories.content: A tombstone is a positive assertion rather than a sentinel. A memory with empty content would be indistinguishable from a serialisation bug.
memories.why: It would leave every reader asking whether a blank record was deliberate, whereas a field naming the act is a claim someone made on purpose.

memories.content: The status scan must peek, not load. Reading metadata and a count has to be a distinct path from opening a store and adding it, because loading a non-current store would union its memories into recall and destroy the entire point of re-pointing.
memories.why: The failure would be silent and in the reassuring direction -- recall working suspiciously well -- so it is worth naming here rather than discovering it.

memories.content: The server is a pure function from a JSON-RPC request to a response, with the transport handled separately in the binary. The tools are then testable without an MCP client or an async runtime, so the parts with decisions in them are exercised directly, and adopting an SDK or a different transport becomes a change to the glue rather than a rewrite of the decisions.
memories.why: Both consequences matter more than the small amount of glue it costs, which is the calculation that makes the separation worth stating rather than discovering.

memories.content: Open: how the inherited and own scores combine. A candidate reached by the walk has the decayed share it inherits from its seed and its own similarity to the query. Both are needed -- the first is what makes traversal worth doing, the second is what makes uniform expansion safe. Whether the result is a maximum, a sum, a weighted blend, or the inherited score acting as a floor changes which memories survive the cut, and the choice is currently unevidenced.
memories.why: This one question replaces most of what per-label traversal behaviour was asking, and it is tractable in a way that question was not: two terms rather than fourteen labels, and a shape that can be measured against a labelled corpus once one exists.

memories.content: Both the why text and the keywords are included in the embedding input by default. The why often surfaces related topics or records of paths not taken, which is exactly what semantic recall should be able to find, and keywords are already curated for topical relevance, so including them is close to free.
memories.why: Measured rather than reasoned: an ablation over a 45-memory labelled corpus with 20 queries put recall at five results at 57.5% for content alone, 65.8% with keywords, 66.7% with why, and 71.7% with both. Both additions help and they compose, so the decision holds on evidence.

memories.content: Decided and built 2026-08-10: a common directory holds stores belonging to every checkout on this machine, defaulting to the home. You separate a store when it is coupled to something that differs between checkouts. A project set is -- it has a working tree and a branch. A cross-project set is not: a lesson learned while reviewing is just as true while developing tomorrow.
memories.why: Set neither and nothing changes, so the simple case degenerates to today's behaviour exactly, which is the property that makes it safe to introduce -- someone who never sets it cannot be affected by it.

memories.content: Scope is single-valued per memory, one enum field rather than a collection. A memory genuinely relevant to more than one project is handled as an explicit cross-reference or duplication.
memories.why: Making it single-valued by construction turns the rule from something discouraged into something untypeable, and the multi-project case is expected to be rare enough not to deserve a field everyone else pays for.

memories.content: What actually associates a set with a directory is the first export or import naming that directory, which records bases against it. That is a real trust-on-first-use record, arrived at by accident rather than by design.
memories.why: A mechanism that exists for one purpose and satisfies another is worth noticing before someone builds the second one from scratch beside it.

memories.content: If any store in the union lacks a model, recall says so rather than quietly answering from the rest -- the same reason a single store says so.
memories.why: Partial results that do not announce themselves are the failure the loud-degradation rule exists to prevent, and the union case is where it would be easiest to let slip, since the answer still looks complete.

memories.content: The secrets clause carries the prohibited-data rule to runtime for the first time. That document asks for the block in both the conventions and, to the extent possible, in software, and as of the drafting neither existed. The convention is the better half to have first: the scan runs at export, by which point the secret is already in the store, where forgetting is the only remedy because a vector is a copy of the text it was built from.
memories.why: Which half of a two-layer defence to build first is decided by where the damage becomes irreversible, and that is upstream of the layer that was specified first.

memories.content: No bulk re-attribution action is designed, because only a human can tell the two cases apart: that was me under a name I no longer use is a label being corrected, while that was someone else is a record being falsified. But the capability exists and is not a workaround -- export the set, edit the identities in the file, import it back, verified end to end with every edited record reconciling cleanly.
memories.why: The route is better placed than a tool action would be. The objection was never that re-attribution is hard; it is that the judgement belongs to a human. Export-edit-import puts a human at exactly that judgement and produces a reviewable diff as the artifact, where a tool action would have to ask the question and accept whatever it was told.

memories.content: Supersession is learned two ways with different availability. Derived from the superseding memory's edge, it requires that memory's set to be loaded, and if it is not, the superseded memory is returned unmarked -- not known at all. Authored as an acknowledgement on the memory itself, it needs nothing, and remains reportable as superseded with the replacement unavailable.
memories.why: This asymmetry decides what can be reported and is the reason the date is not: a date could only ever be reported opportunistically, and a field that is sometimes present teaches the reader to expect it and misleads when it is absent.

memories.content: A memory's outbound degree is fixed when it is written and bounded by how much its author chose to link. Its inbound degree is written by everyone who cites it afterwards, and grows with the corpus. So outbound traversal is self-limiting and inbound traversal is not, which is what the expansion bound exists to contain and why that bound is an inbound concern.
memories.why: The asymmetry is durable rather than incidental, which is what makes it safe to build a bound around.

memories.content: The memory file's header declares a scope, and that declaration is contents -- so it is checked against what the path already established, never used to decide it. A file found in a project's scatterhoard_mem is a project set no matter what its header claims.
memories.why: Otherwise the header is a privilege-escalation channel: a repository declaring local scope would have its memories loaded into the more-trusted local store, escaping the export review gate and outranking genuine local memories under the trust-direction rule.

memories.content: The merge driver is registered against the memory file's name via a gitattributes pattern.
memories.why: That is what makes the name a commitment rather than a convention, since changing it later means every checkout's merge configuration is silently pointing at nothing.
